assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 4 because ID normalization bugs create phantom diffs and broken state handling; frequency is 4 because resource IDs appear in many provider paths; breadth is 4 because the issue spans services and lifecycle stages; hostedDetectability is 4 because parser use and state writes are reviewable in code; evidenceStrength is 5 because the upstream guide explicitly covers scoped and nested IDs; falsePositiveRisk is 1 because the presence or absence of parser normalization is concrete; redundancy is 2 because an active rule exists but misses this explicit scope, so an update is the right action.

assessments.title: Preview fields should not be surfaced until they are GA
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an implementation schema-exposure rule already represented in the Hosted catalog.
assessments.summary: No change: current Hosted rule IMPL-SCHEMA-007 already captures the requirement to keep preview-only properties out of stable schema unless an explicit exception exists.
assessments.impactDescription: Surfacing preview-only fields too early creates unstable practitioner contracts and future compatibility pain.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-SCHEMA-007 already prohibits exposing preview-only Azure properties as stable schema before GA unless the provider's explicit feature-gate policy permits them, which is the Hosted equivalent of the candidate's approved-exception wording.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 3 because preview exposure is important but not always immediately breaking; frequency is 2 because it arises only on preview-backed features; breadth is 3 because multiple services can hit it; hostedDetectability is 4 because preview-version schema additions are visible in diffs; evidenceStrength is 5 because the upstream guidance is direct; falsePositiveRisk is 2 because explicit policy evidence clarifies exceptions; redundancy is 5 because the active Hosted rule already matches the candidate's meaning.
assessments.proposedText: Do not expose preview-only Azure properties as stable schema before GA unless the provider's explicit feature-gate policy permits them.

assessments.title: Represent Azure `None`-style defaults as omission/null in schema design
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an implementation schema-and-state rule already represented in the Hosted catalog.
assessments.summary: No change: current Hosted rule IMPL-SCHEMA-008 already captures the omission-to-sentinel mapping and keeps sentinel values out of user-facing schema semantics.
assessments.impactDescription: Exposing Azure sentinel defaults directly creates awkward UX and can break expand/flatten behavior.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-SCHEMA-008 already requires reviewers to keep `None`/`Off`-style sentinels out of validation, expand omission to the API sentinel, and flatten the sentinel back to omitted state, which is broader and more operational than the candidate wording.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 4 because mishandled sentinels create UX and state defects; frequency is 3 because this pattern appears regularly but not everywhere; breadth is 3 because several Azure services use such defaults; hostedDetectability is 4 because schema, expand, and flatten code reveal the behavior; evidenceStrength is 5 because the upstream guidance is explicit; falsePositiveRisk is 2 because the sentinel semantics are usually clear from the API; redundancy is 5 because the active Hosted rule already covers the same failure condition.
assessments.proposedText: When Azure uses a `None`, `Off`, or equivalent sentinel for omission, keep that sentinel out of user-facing validation, expand omitted configuration to the API sentinel, and flatten the sentinel back to omitted state.

assessments.title: Array schema should use `MinItems` and `MaxItems` when API constraints are known
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an implementation schema-correctness rule whose failure condition is already covered by the existing Hosted schema rule.
assessments.summary: No change: known list cardinality is already part of schema correctness under IMPL-SCHEMA-001, so a separate Hosted rule is unnecessary.
assessments.impactDescription: Missing `MinItems` or `MaxItems` when the API has real cardinality limits allows invalid plans and delays feedback until apply time.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-SCHEMA-001 already instructs reviewers to flag schema declarations that permit invalid requests or reject valid configuration; omitting known list cardinality constraints is one concrete way that defect appears.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 3 because bad cardinality validation causes real but localized schema defects; frequency is 3 because constrained arrays are common but not universal; breadth is 3 because the issue spans multiple services; hostedDetectability is 5 because `MinItems` and `MaxItems` are straightforward to inspect; evidenceStrength is 5 because the upstream guidance is explicit; falsePositiveRisk is 2 because known API limits provide a clear benchmark; redundancy is 4 because the current schema-accuracy rule already covers this defect even though it does not call out cardinality by name.
assessments.proposedText: Required, optional, computed, ForceNew, defaults, conflicts, and validation must match actual API and lifecycle behavior. Flag schema declarations that permit invalid requests, reject valid configuration, or cannot round-trip state.

assessments.title: Optional `TypeList` blocks with no required nested fields need explicit non-empty validation
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an implementation schema-validation rule already represented in the Hosted catalog.
assessments.summary: No change: current Hosted rule IMPL-SCHEMA-010 already captures the need to prevent meaningless empty optional list blocks.
assessments.impactDescription: Allowing empty optional blocks can produce invalid or no-op requests that confuse practitioners and tests.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-SCHEMA-010 already requires an optional `TypeList` block with all-optional nested fields to enforce a non-empty configured item when an empty block would be invalid or meaningless.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 4 because the defect can produce bad requests and misleading config acceptance; frequency is 3 because the pattern appears regularly in nested blocks; breadth is 3 because it spans many services but not all resources; hostedDetectability is 4 because the schema shape is visible in diffs; evidenceStrength is 5 because the upstream guidance and example are direct; falsePositiveRisk is 1 because empty-block invalidity is concrete; redundancy is 5 because the active Hosted rule already covers the same failure condition.
assessments.proposedText: An optional `TypeList` block whose nested fields are all optional must enforce a non-empty configured item when an empty block would produce an invalid or meaningless request.

assessments.title: Flatten single-property `MaxItems: 1` blocks unless there is evidence to keep the wrapper
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a real schema design consideration for implementation review, but the threshold depends on product-shape judgment and future-service knowledge that are hard to enforce reliably in Hosted.
assessments.summary: Defer this rule because it encodes a useful UX preference, but Hosted would need a sharper threshold for when a single-field wrapper is still justified.
assessments.impactDescription: Selecting it now risks false positives on wrappers kept for roadmap, parity, or semantic-clarity reasons that are not visible in a diff.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No current Hosted rule addresses flatten-versus-wrapper schema shape decisions; existing schema rules focus on correctness, validation, and state behavior instead.
assessments.proposedText: Flatten a single-property `MaxItems: 1` wrapper into the parent schema unless evidence shows more sibling properties are imminent or the wrapper carries distinct user-facing semantics; when keeping it, leave a short inline comment explaining why.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 2 because wrapper shape is usually a UX and design issue rather than an immediate bug; frequency is 2 because single-property wrappers are occasional; breadth is 3 because the pattern can recur across services; hostedDetectability is 4 because the schema shape is obvious in code; evidenceStrength is 4 because the upstream guide is explicit; falsePositiveRisk is 5 because reviewer access to future-roadmap evidence is limited; redundancy is 2 because the catalog does not already cover this design heuristic, which supports deferring it instead of forcing a brittle rule.

assessments.title: Portal-required fields should normally be `Required` unless API evidence says otherwise
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a review evidence heuristic relevant to schema assessment, but it is too noisy to enforce as a Hosted rule without clearer authority boundaries.
assessments.summary: Defer this rule because Azure Portal requiredness is a useful signal, but not a reliable enough enforcement source for Hosted on its own.
assessments.impactDescription: If enforced too directly, the rule could generate false positives where the portal is stricter than the API or where provider UX intentionally diverges for valid reasons.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: Current Hosted rules require schema requiredness to match actual behavior through IMPL-SCHEMA-001, but no rule currently treats Azure Portal markers as an enforcement heuristic.
assessments.proposedText: Treat Azure Portal required markers as supporting evidence that a Terraform field should be `Required`; leave such a field `Optional` only when concrete API evidence shows omission is accepted and the resource still works.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 3 because wrong requiredness can cause real schema defects; frequency is 3 because requiredness decisions are common; breadth is 3 because the heuristic could apply widely; hostedDetectability is 2 because Hosted lacks built-in portal context; evidenceStrength is 4 because the upstream guidance is clear about the signal's value; falsePositiveRisk is 4 because portal and API behavior can diverge; redundancy is 3 because IMPL-SCHEMA-001 already covers evidence-backed requiredness without adopting this heuristic, so deferral is safer than updating today.

assessments.title: Use `GetRawConfig()` in `CustomizeDiff` when validation must distinguish configured values from unknown or zero values
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an implementation diff-time validation rule already represented in the Hosted catalog.
assessments.summary: No change: current Hosted rule IMPL-SCHEMA-013 already captures the evidence-backed `GetRawConfig()` and `IsKnown()` safeguards, and the candidate's extra pointer-helper restriction is not strongly sourced enough to expand the rule.
assessments.impactDescription: Getting diff-time unknown handling wrong can cause false validation failures or panics during planning.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-SCHEMA-013 already requires `GetRawConfig()` for optional or unknown values, distinguishes null from configured zero values, and checks `IsKnown()` before traversing collections; that covers the candidate's primary upstream-backed defect pattern.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 5 because bad `CustomizeDiff` handling can panic or reject valid plans; frequency is 3 because not every resource uses diff-time validation; breadth is 3 because the issue spans many optional-value patterns; hostedDetectability is 4 because reviewers can inspect `GetRawConfig()` and raw-value traversal directly; evidenceStrength is 4 because the cited best-practices guidance is strong for the core behavior; falsePositiveRisk is 2 because the main safeguards are concrete; redundancy is 5 because the active Hosted rule already covers the evidenced portion of the candidate.
assessments.proposedText: `CustomizeDiff` validation for optional or unknown values must inspect `GetRawConfig()`, distinguish null from configured zero values, and check `IsKnown()` before traversing collections.

assessments.title: Prefer marketed or portal terminology over raw API names when that improves the Terraform UX
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an implementation naming heuristic with legitimate UX intent, but it is too subjective for reliable Hosted enforcement in its current form.
assessments.summary: Defer this rule because the intent is valid, but terms like 'materially clearer' and 'better user anchor' do not yet define a stable Hosted failure condition.
assessments.impactDescription: Selecting it now could produce inconsistent findings on schema naming choices that require product and ecosystem context beyond the diff.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No current Hosted rule enforces public schema naming preference; existing implementation rules focus on correctness, validation, state, and lifecycle defects.
assessments.proposedText: When a public schema field name differs from the REST API, prefer the clearest Azure-facing term used in the portal or primary CLI unless changed evidence shows another user-facing surface is the better anchor.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 2 because naming clarity matters but usually does not create an immediate functional bug; frequency is 3 because naming decisions recur in schema design; breadth is 3 because many services face API-versus-portal naming differences; hostedDetectability is 3 because changed public field names are visible but the better anchor is not always obvious; evidenceStrength is 4 because the upstream guidance is explicit; falsePositiveRisk is 5 because clarity and user anchor judgments are highly subjective; redundancy is 1 because the catalog does not already cover this naming preference, which supports deferring rather than mapping it onto an unrelated rule.

assessments.title: Group semantically related arguments when a flat schema would scatter one conceptual setting family
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an implementation-schema design expectation for changed Go schema code, so it is within Hosted review scope even though it is not currently selected.
assessments.summary: Exclude from Hosted; the rule is upstream-real but too subjective for a compact defect rule because whether grouping materially reduces cognitive load depends on design judgment and external product-UI context.
assessments.impactDescription: Applying it would push reviewers to challenge flat schemas for UX reasons, but the failure boundary is not binary enough to support low-noise Hosted findings.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No active Hosted rule covers this grouping preference; current schema rules focus on objective API, validation, state, and PATCH defects rather than higher-level schema ergonomics.
assessments.proposedText: When a large flat schema scatters one conceptual setting family, group those related arguments into a block or equivalent shared shape if the portal or CLI treats them as one settings area and the grouped shape better preserves user-facing meaning.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 2 because poor grouping hurts usability more than correctness; frequency 2 because the situation appears mainly in larger schemas; breadth 2 because the effect is mostly on author comprehension; hostedDetectability 1 because reviewers need subjective judgment plus portal or CLI context; evidenceStrength 5 because the guidance is a published upstream standard; falsePositiveRisk 4 because reasonable reviewers can disagree on when grouping is warranted; redundancy 1 because no current Hosted rule already states this design preference.

assessments.title: Avoid ambiguous collection-shaped schemas and name configured blocks by their real cardinality
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This candidate defines an implementation-schema rule that can be checked in changed schema declarations and naming choices.
assessments.summary: Add a Hosted rule for ambiguous collection-shaped schemas and cardinality-based block naming.
assessments.impactDescription: This would let Hosted flag schemas where configuration order implicitly decides a winner or where block names misrepresent whether users configure one object or many.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-SCHEMA-001 can catch resulting invalid behavior, but no current Hosted rule explicitly requires eliminating semantic-slot ambiguity or naming configured blocks by true cardinality.
assessments.proposedText: When repeated Azure items could map multiple configured entries to the same semantic slot, redesign the schema so configuration order cannot decide the winner. Name single configured-object blocks in the singular even if the backing container is list-shaped, and reserve plural names for primitive or computed multi-value collections.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because ambiguous slot resolution can silently apply the wrong user intent; frequency 3 because collection-shaped schema work is common but not universal; breadth 4 because the defect affects configuration, state meaning, and naming clarity; hostedDetectability 4 because duplicate semantic slots and singular-plural mismatches are visible in schema definitions; evidenceStrength 5 because the requirement is backed by published upstream schema and naming guidance; falsePositiveRisk 2 because some edge cases need judgment but the core failure modes are concrete; redundancy 1 because no current Hosted rule states this requirement directly.

assessments.title: Write-only attributes must use symmetric schema relationships and a positive version trigger
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an active Hosted implementation rule sourced from the same upstream guide, and the candidate adds enforceable write-only safeguards missing from the current text.
assessments.summary: Update IMPL-SCHEMA-017 to include supported-field limits and the required create, update, and read handling, not just the symmetric schema relationships and positive version trigger.
assessments.impactDescription: The update would let Hosted catch unsupported write-only shapes and state-drift bugs where `_wo_version` handling or `GetWriteOnly(...)` usage is incomplete.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: Current IMPL-SCHEMA-017 covers symmetric relationships and a positive version trigger, but it does not state the supported-surface limits or the required `GetWriteOnly(...)` and version-state behavior.
assessments.proposedText: Add write-only attributes only for supported sensitive scalar resource fields; require symmetric `ConflictsWith` and `RequiredWith` pairing between `<name>`, `<name>_wo`, and `<name>_wo_version`, validate the version with `validation.IntAtLeast(1)`, use `pluginsdk.GetWriteOnly(...)` on create and trigger-gated update, and persist the configured version trigger in state.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 5 because mistakes here can break secret rotation or leave permanent diffs; frequency 2 because write-only attributes are specialized but recurring; breadth 3 because the rule touches schema, update logic, and state handling; hostedDetectability 4 because the relationships, validator, and state flow are visible in changed code; evidenceStrength 5 because the upstream guide is explicit about these mechanics; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the required patterns are concrete; redundancy 1 because the active rule only partially covers the full enforceable guidance.

assessments.title: Update tests when implementation behavior changes
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The candidate is about repository-level test completeness for code changes, which is related to Hosted review, but it is broader than a single acceptance-test defect pattern.
assessments.summary: Exclude from Hosted; the rule is a broad expectation rather than an independently enforceable defect rule, and the catalog already covers the concrete scenarios where tests are mandatory.
assessments.impactDescription: Adding it would generate generic missing-test findings without enough scenario specificity to distinguish required coverage from acceptable omissions.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-WF-002, TEST-PATTERN-004, TEST-PATTERN-006, TEST-PATTERN-011, and other current testing rules already encode the specific lifecycle and behavior changes that demand acceptance coverage.
assessments.proposedText: When a change materially alters schema behavior, resource behavior, or API mapping, add or update the matching tests instead of leaving the new behavior unexercised.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 3 because missing tests can matter, but the candidate does not identify which behavior changes are truly mandatory; frequency 4 because implementation changes often raise test questions; breadth 4 because it spans many resource and schema changes; hostedDetectability 1 because without scenario-specific criteria Hosted cannot tell required coverage from acceptable omission; evidenceStrength 1 because the candidate is unclassified and cites no concrete source; falsePositiveRisk 5 because a generic missing-test rule would be noisy; redundancy 4 because the catalog already carries narrower test requirements for the important cases.

assessments.title: Prefer ImportStep plus existence checks when appropriate
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a testing-pattern candidate, and current Hosted testing rules already cover its two enforceable parts separately.
assessments.summary: No change; current Hosted testing rules already require existence checks for basic managed-resource tests and prefer `ImportStep()` for broad post-create validation.
assessments.impactDescription: Keeping the current split preserves more precise findings for missing Azure existence checks versus missing import-based validation.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-PATTERN-001 covers `ExistsInAzure` for basic managed-resource tests, and TEST-PATTERN-002 covers preferring `data.ImportStep()` over redundant field assertions.
assessments.proposedText: Basic managed-resource tests must prove Azure existence, normally with `check.That(data.ResourceName).ExistsInAzure(r)`, and broad post-create validation should use `data.ImportStep()` unless field-specific assertions are needed for behavior import cannot prove.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 3 because these are useful acceptance patterns but not the highest-risk defects; frequency 4 because they apply to many managed-resource tests; breadth 3 because they shape assertion style more than overall architecture; hostedDetectability 5 because both patterns are obvious in test code; evidenceStrength 1 because the candidate itself is unclassified; falsePositiveRisk 2 because the existing narrower rules apply cleanly; redundancy 5 because current Hosted coverage already contains both enforceable requirements.

assessments.title: Provider feature-flagged CRUD branch coverage
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is already within Hosted testing scope and maps directly to an active rule about non-default feature-branch coverage.
assessments.summary: No change; TEST-PATTERN-011 already captures the need for focused non-default feature-flag branch coverage.
assessments.impactDescription: Retaining the current rule keeps the same branch-coverage expectation while also preserving the existing safeguard about preparing remote state with `CheckWithClient...` helpers.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-PATTERN-011 already requires one focused acceptance scenario when a provider feature changes CRUD, import, overwrite, or destroy behavior, which matches the candidate's core requirement.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because untested non-default feature branches can hide real lifecycle defects; frequency 2 because feature-gated CRUD changes are periodic rather than constant; breadth 3 because the issue affects changed lifecycle branches in tests; hostedDetectability 5 because the feature branch and its coverage are visible in the diff; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate includes specific local safeguard rationale; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the expectation is concrete and conditional; redundancy 5 because the active Hosted rule already states the same requirement and adds a useful setup safeguard.
assessments.proposedText: When a provider feature changes CRUD, import, overwrite, or destroy behavior, add one focused acceptance scenario for the non-default branch when feasible. Prepare pre-existing remote state with the appropriate `CheckWithClient...` helper instead of a second Terraform resource targeting the same ID.

assessments.title: Prefer typed implementations for new work
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The candidate is a model-selection rule for implementation review, and its enforceable meaning is already carried by an active Hosted rule.
assessments.summary: No change; IMPL-WF-001A already encodes typed-as-default guidance within the broader implementation-model classification rule.
assessments.impactDescription: Keeping the current rule preserves the typed-default expectation while also retaining the needed context about legacy, typed, and framework-native models.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-WF-001A already says to maintain the existing model unless migrating and to use typed for current ordinary resource and data source work.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because choosing the wrong implementation model can derail a change; frequency 3 because new resource and data source work recurs regularly; breadth 4 because the model choice affects many implementation decisions; hostedDetectability 5 because the target surface and implementation style are visible in the repository; evidenceStrength 5 because the guidance is published upstream; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the typed-versus-maintenance distinction is clear; redundancy 5 because IMPL-WF-001A already contains this requirement in broader usable form.
assessments.proposedText: Classify implementation code as legacy untyped Plugin SDK, typed `internal/sdk`, or framework-native before suggesting changes. Maintain the existing model unless the task is an explicit migration; use typed for current ordinary resource and data source work, and framework patterns for framework-native or specialized surfaces.

assessments.title: Identify the implementation model before suggesting code
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This candidate matches an active Hosted model-classification rule, and the remaining extra detail is mostly workflow elaboration rather than missing defect criteria.
assessments.summary: No change; current IMPL-WF-001A already preserves the enforceable model-classification behavior, and the candidate's extra poller-skill pointer is workflow guidance rather than a Hosted defect rule.
assessments.impactDescription: Keeping the current text preserves low-noise model classification while avoiding a broader instruction that mixes code-review findings with internal workflow routing.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The active IMPL-WF-001A already covers legacy vs typed vs framework classification, matching existing-model maintenance, typed preference for ordinary new work, and framework handling for specialized surfaces.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because bad model classification leads to the wrong implementation advice; frequency 3 because reviewers encounter mixed models regularly; breadth 4 because the rule affects many later implementation calls; hostedDetectability 5 because file location and APIs reveal the model; evidenceStrength 5 because the candidate cites upstream and maintainer-backed sources; falsePositiveRisk 2 because the current condensed rule is already precise enough for review; redundancy 4 because most of the candidate's enforceable content is already in the active Hosted rule.
assessments.proposedText: Classify implementation code as legacy untyped Plugin SDK, typed `internal/sdk`, or framework-native before suggesting changes. Maintain the existing model unless the task is an explicit migration; use typed for current ordinary resource and data source work, and framework patterns for framework-native or specialized surfaces.

assessments.title: New resources must include resource identity and list-resource planning
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a cross-file repository workflow rule for new resources, and Hosted can evaluate it from diffs that introduce a new managed resource and omit required companion work.
assessments.summary: Add a Hosted repository rule that new resources must plan Resource Identity and a companion list resource by default, with only documented exception paths allowing omission.
assessments.impactDescription: This would let Hosted flag new-resource PRs that add the primary resource but silently skip required identity, list-resource, test, or documentation work.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: Current Hosted rules cover callback identity details and list-resource query tests once those surfaces exist, but no rule requires the new-resource workflow to include Resource Identity plus a companion list resource or an explicit exception path.
assessments.proposedText: A new managed resource should ship with Resource Identity support and a companion list resource by default. Missing list support requires the documented maintainer-reviewed exception path, not silent omission, and the change should include the needed implementation, tests, and docs for that workflow.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 5 because upstream treats these as mandatory prerequisites for new resources; frequency 3 because new-resource work is meaningful but not constant; breadth 5 because the rule spans code, tests, docs, and CI expectations; hostedDetectability 4 because a new-resource PR clearly shows whether the companion work is present or explicitly excepted; evidenceStrength 5 because the guidance is explicit in published upstream documents; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the exception path is concrete; redundancy 1 because no current Hosted rule requires this workflow end to end.

assessments.title: Existing resources retrofitting list support should add the full companion set together
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a repository-level rule for list-support retrofits that can be checked when a PR explicitly adds list support to an existing resource.
assessments.summary: Add a Hosted repository rule requiring existing-resource list-support retrofits to ship the full companion set together.
assessments.impactDescription: This would catch partial retrofits that add a list implementation but omit Resource Identity, registration, query coverage, or list-resource documentation.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No current Hosted rule covers the completeness of retrofitting list support onto an existing resource; TEST-WF-003 only governs query coverage for a new list resource after it exists.
assessments.proposedText: When explicitly retrofitting list support onto an existing resource, add the full companion set together: Resource Identity, the `*_resource_list.go` implementation and registration, list-query acceptance coverage, and list-resource docs.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because a partial retrofit leaves a provider pattern incomplete and user-facing support fragmented; frequency 2 because retrofits are narrower than new resources; breadth 4 because the workflow spans implementation, registration, tests, and docs; hostedDetectability 4 because a list-support PR makes the missing companions visible; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate combines upstream workflow guidance with a concrete provider PR example; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the trigger is specific to explicit list-support retrofits; redundancy 1 because the current catalog does not express this completeness requirement.

assessments.title: Create-time import checks must honor the overwrite feature gate
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an active Hosted implementation rule from the same upstream source, and the candidate adds enforceable branch details that the current text omits.
assessments.summary: Update IMPL-WF-002B to spell out the safe existence-probe branches around the overwrite feature gate.
assessments.impactDescription: The update would let Hosted catch implementations that honor the flag but still mishandle `404` or swallow unexpected GET failures in create-time import checks.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: Current IMPL-WF-002B captures the feature-gate requirement, but it does not state that `404` must still proceed to create and unexpected GET failures must still return an error.
assessments.proposedText: When create probes for an existing resource, return `tf.ImportAsExistsError(...)` only for the feature-disabled found-existing branch; still return unexpected GET failures as errors, allow `404` to proceed to create, and skip import-as-exists when `SkipImportCheckOnCreateAndAllowOverwritingExistingResources` is enabled.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because mishandling this branch changes create semantics and can mask real failures; frequency 3 because create-time existence checks are common in resources; breadth 3 because the rule affects a focused create-path branch; hostedDetectability 5 because the relevant branches are explicit in code; evidenceStrength 5 because the upstream example is specific; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the expected control flow is concrete; redundancy 2 because the current rule covers the headline feature gate but not these safety branches.

assessments.title: Callback-based create flows must set identity when Resource Identity is supported
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an active Hosted implementation rule from the same upstream guidance, and the candidate expands it with enforceable create-path details that are still in scope.
assessments.summary: Update IMPL-WF-002C so it covers both callback-based and non-callback create paths that must set identity in create rather than deferring to `Read`.
assessments.impactDescription: The update would catch callback helpers that only set ID as well as ordinary create flows that leave required identity population for a later read.

assessments.title: New resources must include the required documentation companions

assessments.title: Use an existing local base

assessments.proposedText: When drafting a PR description, select the first usable local base in order `upstream/main`, `origin/main`, then local `main`, do not refresh remote-tracking refs, and record the chosen ref and commit in the handoff.

assessments.title: Diff from the merge base

assessments.proposedText: If the initial merge-base scope is implausibly broad, run one bounded local recovery pass, derive at most one candidate origin from clear mainline integration or a contiguous contributor tip stack, and replace the base only when the candidate is an ancestor of `HEAD` and yields a strictly narrower non-empty scope.

assessments.title: Explain what and why

Give a companion change a separate line only when repository evidence proves distinct user-facing behavior beyond the main change.

assessments.title: No finding may be silently dropped by the advocate pass

assessments.proposedText: Do not add Hosted rules for whether an internal advocate pass deletes, hides, or replaces stored findings; that retention behavior is out of scope.

assessments.title: Mandatory-source requirement for architectural Issues
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is cross-cutting review-classification guidance that can be enforced from the review text itself and does not depend on hidden architect-pass mechanics. The current Hosted catalog has evidence rules for factual claims, but no rule that architectural issues require a cited mandatory source.
assessments.summary: Add a Hosted rule that architectural concerns may be raised as issues only when a mandatory repository or Hosted source is directly cited.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this rule, Hosted review can overstate design preferences or stylistic ideas as blocking architectural issues even when no mandatory source requires the change.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: `IMPL-EVID-001` and `DOCS-EVID-001` limit unsupported factual claims inside their surfaces, but no current Hosted rule governs when an architectural concern may escalate from observation to issue.
assessments.proposedText: Raise an architectural issue only when the reviewed change violates a mandatory contributor, maintainer, or Hosted rule that you can cite directly. If the concern is a preference, stylistic improvement, or unsupported design alternative, keep it as an observation and do not present it as a requirement.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity 4 fits because unsupported architectural issues can block correct changes and distort moderation outcomes; frequency 3 fits because design-preference comments recur on structural work; breadth 3 fits because the rule can affect implementation, testing, and documentation reviews whenever architecture is discussed; hostedDetectability 3 fits because the presence or absence of a cited mandatory source is visible in review text; evidenceStrength 2 fits because the contract expresses the requirement clearly even though the batch provides no separate upstream corroboration; falsePositiveRisk 2 fits because the rule fires only when a reviewer escalates a preference without mandatory support; redundancy 1 fits because no current Hosted rule covers this issue-versus-observation boundary for architecture.

assessments.title: Respect change-set scope boundaries
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This candidate expresses a general review-skill safeguard about not blocking an otherwise acceptable change for failing to perform a broader refactor outside the submitted scope. That principle is enforceable from the review itself and is not tied to hidden workflow state.
assessments.summary: Add a Hosted rule that keeps architectural feedback in scope and downgrades broader redesign demands to observations.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this rule, Hosted review can turn preferred larger refactors into blocking feedback against self-consistent changes that did not attempt the broader redesign.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No current Hosted rule prevents architecture feedback from blocking on preferred but out-of-scope redesigns.
assessments.proposedText: Do not raise an architectural issue solely to demand a broad refactor beyond the reviewed change-set. When the submitted change is self-consistent and evidence-acceptable, record larger preferred redesigns as observations rather than blocking issues.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity 3 fits because out-of-scope blocking architecture feedback can materially slow correct changes; frequency 3 fits because broader redesign requests recur on structural work; breadth 3 fits because this can affect any review surface when architecture is discussed; hostedDetectability 2 fits because explicit demands for broad refactors are visible but scope judgments remain somewhat subjective; evidenceStrength 2 fits because the contract states the rule clearly without separate upstream confirmation in the batch; falsePositiveRisk 3 fits because legitimate in-scope structural defects must still be reportable; redundancy 2 fits because the catalog lacks this scope-boundary safeguard even though it is adjacent to the mandatory-source classification rule.

assessments.title: Run azurerm-linter when the scoped changes include provider Go files
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This candidate tells the review runner when to execute `azurerm-linter` and how to classify non-applicable runs. That is executor behavior, not a Hosted repository review rule.

assessments.title: Prefer JSON payloads when available
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an enforceable rule for authoritative linter evidence selection and minimum supported JSON review mode, which belongs in Hosted review-classification guidance.

assessments.impactDescription: This prevents Hosted reviews from scraping noisy text when structured evidence exists and blocks false confidence from unsupported JSON modes or obsolete binaries.

assessments.title: azurerm-linter findings are reported as issues
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a core review-classification rule that governs how confirmed azurerm-linter findings must appear in Hosted review output.
assessments.summary: Add a rule that confirmed azurerm-linter findings must surface as review issues and cannot be buried inside execution metadata or suppressed by contributor preference.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this requirement, a Hosted review could acknowledge linter findings in tooling output yet fail to present them as actionable review results, hiding blocking evidence from downstream consumers.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no rule requiring azurerm-linter findings to remain visible as review issues.
assessments.proposedText: When azurerm-linter reports findings for the executed scope, surface them as review issues and actionable linter entries. Do not suppress, downgrade, or hide them because the executed scope differs from the reviewed diff; disclose any scope mismatch instead.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 5 because hiding or downgrading known linter findings can directly suppress blocking review outcomes; frequency 4 because scope mismatches and pressure to collapse payload-only findings are realistic in review pipelines; breadth 3 because the rule affects all linter-backed reviews but not unrelated code-review paths; hostedDetectability 4 because the presence of findings and their absence from surfaced issues is observable; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate is explicit about the required failure condition and exception handling; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the rule applies only after the linter has already reported findings; redundancy 1 because no current Hosted rule covers this visibility requirement.

assessments.title: Populate scope and failure reasons explicitly
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The subject is in scope for review-classification guidance, but this candidate bundles several separable concernsΓÇöscope disclosure, `Not run` reasons, install hints, Windows execution claims, and payload field layoutΓÇöinto one compound rule.
assessments.summary: Defer this candidate until the linter review surface is split into smaller enforceable rules.
assessments.impactDescription: The underlying ideas are useful, but adding them as one Hosted rule would create an over-broad requirement with mixed classification, execution, and presentation obligations.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: Current Hosted coverage has no linter-payload surface, and the adjacent candidate set already proposes narrower rules for parse errors, JSON authority, zero-findings handling, scope matching, and finding visibility.
assessments.proposedText: When reporting `azurerm-linter`, state the reviewed scope and, if it did not run, give the concrete reason. Do not omit the tool or imply success when no classifiable run occurred.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because several clauses affect whether Hosted review correctly explains linter execution; frequency 4 because scope and failure-summary handling are common concerns in linter-backed reviews; breadth 4 because the candidate touches multiple parts of the linter flow; hostedDetectability 2 because the bundled rule mixes observable statuses with less directly testable presentation and execution claims; evidenceStrength 3 because the individual ideas are concrete but the candidate combines too many obligations into one unit; falsePositiveRisk 3 because enforcing it as written would require subjective judgments about payload shape and platform claims; redundancy 4 because much of the semantic core overlaps narrower linter candidates that are better fits for standalone Hosted rules.

assessments.title: Populate the linter payload from actual tool output
assessments.applicabilityRationale: As written, this candidate combines evidence handling with renderer-specific payload fields, empty-state markers, Markdown link labels, and presentation formatting that are too implementation-specific for a reusable Hosted rule.
assessments.summary: Exclude this renderer-specific linter payload construction candidate from the Hosted catalog.
assessments.impactDescription: Encoding exact payload and link-shape details here would overfit the Hosted catalog to one downstream presentation format and make future linter plumbing harder to change safely.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no review-workflow rule in this area, and the reusable semantic core is better captured by narrower rules for JSON authority and finding preservation rather than exact field and link formatting.
assessments.proposedText: Build the linter summary and findings from actual `azurerm-linter` output. Treat only reported violations as actionable findings, and do not promote preamble or cleanup logs into findings.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 2 because the candidate mainly affects payload shape and readability rather than the existence of a core code-review finding; frequency 3 because linter payload construction recurs wherever the tool runs; breadth 2 because the rule is tightly scoped to one formatter path; hostedDetectability 2 because many clauses depend on exact output-shape preferences rather than simple semantic checks; evidenceStrength 3 because the candidate is detailed but tied to a local payload contract instead of broader Hosted guidance; falsePositiveRisk 4 because enforcing exact link labels and empty-state formatting would create noisy failures with little review value; redundancy 4 because its semantic core overlaps narrower, better-targeted linter candidates while the extra formatting detail is not Hosted-worthy.

assessments.title: Normalize finding lines when possible
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an enforceable evidence-preservation rule for how Hosted review should carry azurerm-linter findings forward without guessing paths.
assessments.summary: Add a rule that actionable azurerm-linter findings must preserve the reported check ID, location, and message, while normalizing temporary worktree paths only when that mapping is deterministic.
assessments.impactDescription: This keeps linter evidence trustworthy and reviewable by preventing path guessing while still improving usability when repo-relative normalization is provable.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no rule for preserving azurerm-linter finding identity or for deterministic path normalization from temporary worktrees.
assessments.proposedText: Each actionable azurerm-linter finding must preserve the reported check ID, file path, line number, and message. Normalize temporary worktree paths to deterministic repo-relative paths when possible, and otherwise keep the raw path rather than guessing.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 3 because incorrect or guessed finding locations weaken evidence quality and can misdirect remediation; frequency 3 because temporary worktree paths and location normalization are plausible in review execution; breadth 2 because the rule is limited to azurerm-linter-backed output handling; hostedDetectability 3 because path preservation and normalization behavior can be checked from emitted findings but still requires some context; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate states a crisp preserve-or-keep-raw boundary; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the rule prefers raw evidence over guessing; redundancy 2 because it complements, but does not duplicate, the broader JSON-authority and linter-visibility candidates.

assessments.title: Persist and inspect full linter output deterministically
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This candidate is about executor artifact hygiene and debug-file handling, not about a reusable Hosted review judgment or evidence-classification rule.
assessments.summary: Exclude temporary log-file and helper-script hygiene from the Hosted rule catalog.
assessments.impactDescription: These requirements constrain how the review runner is implemented, but they do not define whether a review correctly classifies or reports repository defects.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog intentionally does not govern temporary artifact management or system-temp execution mechanics.
assessments.proposedText: Normal review runs must not rely on persistent temporary linter logs or helper scripts. Any debug artifacts must be deliberate and removed before the review completes.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 1 because the rule mainly affects execution cleanliness rather than review correctness; frequency 2 because temp artifacts may appear in some runs but are not universal; breadth 1 because the concern is narrowly about one implementation detail of the runner; hostedDetectability 1 because temporary file behavior is not reliably inferable from normal review output; evidenceStrength 3 because the candidate is explicit about the desired operational behavior; falsePositiveRisk 5 because trying to enforce runner hygiene as a Hosted review rule would be noisy and under-evidenced; redundancy 2 because the concern is distinct but belongs in execution tooling guidance rather than the Hosted catalog.

assessments.title: Do not claim absence without searching the full saved output
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This candidate depends on a specific persisted-log workflow and saved-output search process that the Hosted catalog does not standardize.
assessments.summary: Exclude the saved-output search requirement from the Hosted catalog.
assessments.impactDescription: The broad evidence-integrity idea is useful, but binding Hosted guidance to a particular saved-log workflow would over-specify one executor implementation path.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no rule that standardizes persisted linter transcripts or saved-output search mechanics.
assessments.proposedText: Do not claim that `azurerm-linter` omitted a specific file or rule unless the complete linter output was checked for that file path or rule ID.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 2 because unsupported absence claims can mislead review conclusions but this candidate addresses that risk through one specific operational method; frequency 2 because explicit absence claims for a particular rule or file are narrower than general linter handling; breadth 1 because the rule is tied to a saved-output workflow; hostedDetectability 2 because verifying whether a reviewer searched a complete saved transcript is difficult from final output alone; evidenceStrength 2 because the candidate states a method but not a reusable Hosted abstraction; falsePositiveRisk 4 because enforcement would depend on unobserved runner behavior; redundancy 2 because the concern is distinct but not suitable for the Hosted surface.

assessments.title: Prefer exact review-scope linting
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a compact, enforceable rule about matching linter execution scope to the review target and disclosing deviations.
assessments.summary: Add a rule that azurerm-linter should run against the intended review scope as closely as possible and must disclose any broader or narrower executed scope.
assessments.impactDescription: This keeps linter evidence calibrated to the reviewed change and prevents hidden scope drift from being mistaken for exact diff coverage.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no rule for aligning azurerm-linter execution scope with the selected review scope.
assessments.proposedText: Run azurerm-linter against the selected review scope as closely as the tool supports. If the executed scope is broader or narrower, disclose that mismatch in the linter summary.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 3 because scope drift mainly affects evidence interpretation rather than creating a finding by itself; frequency 4 because exact diff scoping is a recurring challenge in automated lint review; breadth 3 because the rule affects most azurerm-linter-backed reviews; hostedDetectability 3 because the intended and executed scopes can usually be compared but may need prompt context; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate states a simple preference and fallback disclosure requirement; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the rule allows approximation and only requires explicit disclosure when exact scope is unavailable; redundancy 2 because it overlaps slightly with the linter-findings visibility rule's scope-mismatch clause but adds an execution-side expectation.

assessments.title: Moderator synthesizes existing workflow findings, not a new independent review
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a core review-classification rule for moderation behavior and evidence boundaries in a multi-pass Hosted review workflow.
assessments.summary: Add a rule that moderation synthesizes structured findings from earlier passes instead of replacing them with a new evidence-free audit.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this boundary, the moderation step can invent unsupported findings, erase upstream work, or leave explicit zero-finding inputs without a deterministic owner.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no moderation rule defining whether the final pass may create a fresh independent audit or how it handles an explicit empty input set.
assessments.proposedText: Moderator review must synthesize the structured findings produced by earlier workflow passes rather than replacing them with a new independent audit. Do not invent unsupported findings, and treat an explicit empty input record set as a valid zero-findings finalization.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because allowing moderation to invent or replace findings can materially distort final review outcomes; frequency 4 because every multi-pass moderated review depends on this ownership boundary; breadth 4 because the rule affects the whole moderated review workflow, not one repository surface; hostedDetectability 3 because divergence between input records and final output is inspectable but not trivial; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate defines the moderation role and empty-set behavior directly; falsePositiveRisk 2 because the rule is conceptually broad but still anchored to structured workflow inputs; redundancy 1 because the Hosted catalog currently has no moderation guidance.

assessments.title: Moderator consumes the shared handoff schema
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an enforceable workflow-evidence rule about preserving structured moderation records and treating explicit empty inputs as valid.
assessments.summary: Add a rule that moderation must preserve the shared structured finding schema instead of collapsing records into prose.
assessments.impactDescription: This protects record identity, evidence, confidence, and classification fields that downstream stages need to render and reason about final findings consistently.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no rule for preserving shared workflow finding schema fields across moderation.
assessments.proposedText: Moderator input and output must preserve the shared workflow finding record schema. The moderator may enrich metadata, but must not replace structured records with prose that drops identity, scope, evidence, reasoning, confidence, classification, or visibility; an explicit empty record set remains a valid moderation input.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because losing structured fields can break evidence integrity and downstream rendering of final findings; frequency 3 because schema-preservation failures are less constant than general moderation decisions but still central when they occur; breadth 4 because the rule affects all moderated workflow records; hostedDetectability 4 because dropped fields and schema replacement are directly observable in the handoff payload; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate names the required preserved fields and allowed enrichments; falsePositiveRisk 1 because schema preservation is concrete and machine-checkable; redundancy 2 because it complements the broader moderation-ownership rule without duplicating it.

assessments.title: Moderator owns deterministic presentation hints for surviving findings
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This candidate is dominated by downstream presentation-shape, title-casing, and renderer fallback details rather than a compact, reusable Hosted review rule.
assessments.summary: Exclude detailed presentation-hint ownership and title-formatting requirements from the Hosted catalog.
assessments.impactDescription: Most of this candidate specifies how one presentation layer should populate and style finding cards, which is too renderer-coupled for the Hosted semantic rule set.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog does not include presentation-layer formatting rules, and the reusable moderation semantics are better captured by schema-preservation and evidence-bound normalization rules.
assessments.proposedText: When a surviving finding needs structured presentation fields, populate only fields that are deterministically supported by the finding and its evidence. Do not invent summaries, impacts, evidence blocks, suggested changes, or code snippets for downstream rendering.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 2 because the candidate mainly affects final presentation polish and completeness rather than whether a substantive review finding exists; frequency 3 because every moderated finding may carry presentation data; breadth 3 because the clauses span summaries, evidence blocks, and code snippets but remain presentation-centric; hostedDetectability 3 because missing or differently cased presentation fields are observable; evidenceStrength 3 because the candidate is detailed but tied to a local rendering contract; falsePositiveRisk 4 because enforcing title case and card-shape specifics as Hosted rules would create noisy non-semantic failures; redundancy 4 because much of the meaningful moderation behavior is already better handled by broader schema and evidence rules.

assessments.title: Moderator owns final visibility
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This candidate is primarily a component-ownership contract between moderator and downstream renderer layers, not a reusable Hosted review judgment rule.
assessments.summary: Exclude moderator visibility-field ownership from the Hosted catalog.
assessments.impactDescription: The rule governs which pipeline component may flip `visible` flags, but that is orchestration plumbing rather than a standalone semantic review requirement.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog intentionally has no pipeline ownership rules for visibility toggling or renderer override behavior.
assessments.proposedText: Moderator-owned visibility is authoritative: findings kept in the final review must remain visible, and records absorbed into a true duplicate merge must be hidden and linked to the surviving record.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 2 because incorrect visibility ownership can confuse workflow output but is one layer removed from the core validity of the finding itself; frequency 3 because visibility is relevant for every moderated record; breadth 3 because the rule affects final review assembly across the workflow; hostedDetectability 3 because conflicting `visible` states and override behavior are observable in structured records; evidenceStrength 3 because the candidate states a clear ownership boundary; falsePositiveRisk 4 because enforcing component ownership in the Hosted catalog would rely on pipeline architecture choices rather than review semantics; redundancy 3 because broader moderation and schema rules already cover most of the durable semantic value.

assessments.title: Moderator owns visible issue and observation semantics
assessments.applicabilityRationale: As written, this candidate is a workflow-layer ownership split between moderator, generic prompts, and render-only presentation rather than a direct Hosted review rule.
assessments.summary: Exclude downstream ownership-splitting for issue and observation presentation from the Hosted catalog.
assessments.impactDescription: The semantic goal is sensible, but the candidate mostly prescribes which pipeline layer may reinterpret classifications after moderation, which is too orchestration-specific for Hosted guidance.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no prompt-layer or renderer-layer ownership rules for post-moderation classification transport.
assessments.proposedText: The moderator is the sole authority for whether a surviving concern appears in the final review and whether it is classified as an issue or observation. Downstream presentation must preserve that decision rather than reclassifying it.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 3 because post-moderation reclassification can alter final review outcomes, but the candidate addresses that through internal workflow ownership boundaries; frequency 3 because classification transport recurs in moderated review flows; breadth 3 because the rule spans issue and observation placement across the pipeline; hostedDetectability 3 because conflicting classifications are observable but proving which component caused them is less direct; evidenceStrength 3 because the ownership intent is explicit; falsePositiveRisk 4 because cataloging component boundaries as Hosted rules would create architecture-dependent failures; redundancy 3 because the durable semantic core is better captured by moderation-ownership and evidence-bound normalization rules.

assessments.title: Duplicate concerns merge into one strongest record
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an enforceable moderation rule for deduplicating truly identical concerns while preserving distinct evidence-backed defects as separate findings.
assessments.summary: Add a rule that moderation must merge genuine duplicate concerns into one strongest surviving record without collapsing distinct defects that only share files or evidence.
assessments.impactDescription: This prevents double-counting the same issue while protecting materially different concerns from being erased during over-aggressive deduplication.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no rule for duplicate-merge semantics, surviving-record requirements, or `mergedInto` tracking.
assessments.proposedText: When multiple workflow records describe the same underlying concern, merge them into one surviving record that keeps the strongest evidence, the narrowest defensible claim, and the combined attribution. Do not merge records that prove different defects merely because they touch the same files or objects, and mark absorbed duplicates with `mergedInto`.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because duplicate handling can materially inflate or erase final findings; frequency 4 because overlap between independent workflow passes is common in moderated review systems; breadth 4 because the rule affects the whole final-finding assembly process; hostedDetectability 3 because duplicate merges and missing distinct records are inspectable but require comparing reasoning and evidence; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate gives clear keep-separate and merge-together boundaries; falsePositiveRisk 2 because some duplicate judgments are nuanced but the rule still anchors to shared underlying concern; redundancy 1 because the Hosted catalog has no existing deduplication rule.

assessments.title: Severity and wording normalization are evidence-bound
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a general review-classification rule for moderation that constrains severity and wording changes to what the evidence supports.
assessments.summary: Add a rule that moderation may normalize severity or wording only within the bounds of proved evidence and should prefer the narrower defensible claim.
assessments.impactDescription: This reduces speculative escalation, keeps final findings faithful to the record, and prevents moderation from broadening a claim beyond what the evidence proves.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no moderation rule for evidence-bound normalization or for preferring narrower defensible phrasing.
assessments.proposedText: Moderator severity and wording changes must stay evidence-bound. When multiple phrasings are plausible, prefer the narrower defensible claim and keep each surviving record in exactly one final classification.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because unsupported normalization can materially distort how serious a final finding appears; frequency 4 because wording and severity edits are routine moderation actions; breadth 4 because the rule applies across all moderated findings; hostedDetectability 3 because over-broad phrasing can be reviewed against the source record but is not purely mechanical; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate states a concise evidence boundary and narrower-claim preference; falsePositiveRisk 2 because there is some judgment in comparing plausible phrasings; redundancy 1 because the Hosted catalog currently has no equivalent moderation-normalization rule.

assessments.title: Critical versus high severity is determined by present destructive or catastrophic harm
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an enforceable severity-classification rule that defines the boundary between `critical` and `high` for moderated Hosted findings.
assessments.summary: Add a rule that reserves `critical` for findings with current-run proof of destructive, catastrophic, or severe trust-boundary harm and keeps other blocking correctness defects at `high`.
assessments.impactDescription: This prevents severity inflation while still preserving strong escalation when the review record proves active destructive behavior or catastrophic trust-boundary failure.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no rule defining when moderated findings should be `critical` versus `high`.
assessments.proposedText: Use `critical` severity only when current-run evidence proves a present destructive, catastrophic, or severe trust-boundary failure. Use `high` for blocking correctness defects that remain serious but do not yet prove catastrophic or destructive harm.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 5 because the `critical` versus `high` boundary strongly affects how final findings are prioritized and consumed; frequency 3 because truly severe findings are less common than ordinary issues but still important; breadth 3 because the rule applies only to higher-severity moderation decisions, not every record; hostedDetectability 3 because current-run destructive evidence can be checked but often requires multi-record reasoning; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate provides a concrete severity threshold and examples; falsePositiveRisk 2 because severity assessment still involves some interpretive judgment; redundancy 2 because it builds on, but does not duplicate, the broader evidence-bound normalization rule.

assessments.title: Moderator consumes advocate commentary without inventing a second advocate pass
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This candidate is narrowly tied to one multi-role workflow variant and its `roleNotes` plumbing rather than a general Hosted review rule.
assessments.summary: Exclude advocate-pass-specific commentary handling from the Hosted catalog.
assessments.impactDescription: The rule depends on a particular advocate-role workflow and record field, so cataloging it would over-specialize Hosted guidance to one orchestration pattern.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no advocate-role workflow rules or `roleNotes`-specific preservation requirements.
assessments.proposedText: When advocate commentary is part of the workflow, treat it as upstream moderation input and preserve it on surviving records. Do not invent a second advocate pass or erase preserved commentary during normalization.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 2 because losing advocate commentary can reduce context but usually does not by itself create or erase the core defect evidence; frequency 2 because the rule only matters when an advocate-role pass is present; breadth 2 because it affects one specialized workflow branch; hostedDetectability 2 because missing commentary preservation is harder to prove from final output alone; evidenceStrength 3 because the candidate clearly describes the intended handling; falsePositiveRisk 4 because enforcing role-specific orchestration details as Hosted rules would be noisy outside that workflow; redundancy 2 because the concern is distinct but too specialized for the general catalog.

assessments.title: Presentation hints are evidence-bound
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a cross-surface review-quality safeguard: Hosted needs a rule that forbids unsupported summary, remediation, or classification drift after findings are generated and merged.
assessments.summary: The candidate adds a missing post-processing evidence rule for normalized findings and duplicate merges.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this safeguard, moderation can embellish fixes, overstate impact, or drop issue-class lineage even when the underlying repository evidence is narrower.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-EVID-001, TEST-EVID-001, and DOCS-EVID-001 require evidence for repository claims, but no current Hosted rule governs evidence-preserving enrichment or duplicate-merge lineage after findings are produced.
assessments.proposedText: Do not strengthen a finding's summary, impact, evidence, suggested change, or code example beyond what the cited defect evidence proves. When merging duplicate findings, preserve the supported issue classification lineage from each source finding.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 4 because embellished remediation or lost classification lineage can materially mislead developers even when the original finding was valid. Frequency is 3 because normalization and deduplication are common in synthesized reviews but not every run needs them. Breadth is 4 because the safeguard applies across implementation, testing, and documentation findings. Hosted detectability is 3 because unsupported enrichment and dropped lineage are reviewable in the final record set but require comparing the prose to the cited evidence. Evidence strength is 3 because the rule comes from an active internal contract and aligns with the catalog's existing evidence discipline, but it lacks separate upstream or maintainer citation. False-positive risk is 2 because reviewers can usually tell when added remediation or classification goes beyond the proved defect. Redundancy is 1 because the current catalog has per-surface evidence rules but no cross-surface moderation rule for post-processing fidelity.

assessments.title: Final synthesis stays inside the downstream output contract
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This governs moderator authority, stage ordering, rendering ownership, and empty-result workflow behavior rather than an independently enforceable Hosted rule about reviewing repository changes or classifying defects.
assessments.summary: The candidate is a workflow-orchestration contract for the moderator stage, not a Hosted review rule.
assessments.impactDescription: Its failure would change who renders the final body or how an empty moderation stage is finalized, but it would not directly change whether Hosted correctly identifies a repository defect.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog intentionally stops at repository review guidance and does not encode moderator-stage routing, rendering ownership, or output-section authority.
assessments.proposedText: Moderation may merge and normalize findings, but it must not rewrite the authorized final review structure or add new reader-visible sections. An explicit empty moderated result is still a completed moderation outcome, not a skipped stage.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 2 because incorrect ownership or stage handling affects workflow determinism more than defect quality. Frequency is 2 because moderation is not universal across all Hosted review flows. Breadth is 1 because the rule applies only to a specific internal stage boundary. Hosted detectability is 4 because the unauthorized extra section or renderer behavior would usually be obvious in output. Evidence strength is 1 because the candidate has no upstream or maintainer corroboration in the current catalog inputs. False-positive risk is 4 because model-based review would struggle to distinguish prompt authority mistakes from acceptable orchestration changes. Redundancy is 3 because the candidate mostly restates pipeline contracts that sit outside the catalog's review-rule scope.

assessments.title: Moderator routing must stay explicit
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a prompt-routing and execution-order rule for an internal moderation pass, not a Hosted instruction about repository review behavior.
assessments.summary: The candidate belongs to workflow routing, not the Hosted review catalog.
assessments.impactDescription: A violation would mean the system reported moderator execution inaccurately or ran it at the wrong stage, but it would not by itself define a code-review defect against the repository.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No active Hosted rule covers prompt-stage routing because the catalog focuses on reviewable repository content and evidence-backed findings.
assessments.proposedText: Claim that a moderator pass ran only when the prompt explicitly routed that pass. When used, run moderation after finding-generation and commentary stages and before the final review is frozen.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 2 because incorrect routing affects process integrity more than defect semantics. Frequency is 2 because only workflows with a moderator pass are affected. Breadth is 1 because the rule is limited to one orchestration feature. Hosted detectability is 5 because explicit route claims and stage placement are usually easy to inspect. Evidence strength is 1 because the candidate is unclassified and unsupported by other catalog evidence. False-positive risk is 3 because some prompt changes could legitimately alter stage ordering without creating a review-quality issue. Redundancy is 2 because the catalog already excludes this kind of orchestration detail.

assessments.title: Moderator output is final synthesis, not role narration
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This controls final-body narration style for a specific internal role rather than an independently enforceable rule about defect evidence, repository correctness, or Hosted review classification.
assessments.summary: The candidate is output-style guidance for moderator narration, not a Hosted review rule.
assessments.impactDescription: A violation would add internal-process commentary to the review body, but it would not change the substantive correctness of repository findings.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The Hosted catalog does not regulate role narration or final-body exposition style for internal workflow stages.
assessments.proposedText: The final review must present normalized findings, not internal moderator process narration. Any visible moderator trace must come only through authorized findings or verification markers.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 1 because the failure is mostly cosmetic and explanatory. Frequency is 2 because moderator-visible narration can recur whenever that role runs. Breadth is 1 because it affects only one output style convention. Hosted detectability is 4 because explicit process narration is usually visible in the rendered text. Evidence strength is 1 because no separate catalog evidence supports elevating this to Hosted guidance. False-positive risk is 4 because distinguishing unacceptable narration from acceptable concise context would be subjective. Redundancy is 3 because the catalog intentionally avoids stylistic role-output rules.

assessments.title: Moderator output may prepare the render-only presentation layer
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The candidate addresses a real Hosted concern: auxiliary presentation metadata must not become a second finding taxonomy. But it is tightly coupled to the specific moderator-to-renderer handoff design.
assessments.summary: The semantic boundary between presentation hints and actual classification is relevant, but the rule is too architecture-specific to add unchanged.
assessments.impactDescription: If presentation hints drift into a second taxonomy, readers can see inconsistent severities or review types even when the base finding set is correct.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has evidence rules for finding validity but no dedicated rule for subordinate presentation metadata or moderator handoff semantics.
assessments.proposedText: Presentation hints may enrich a surviving finding, but they must remain subordinate to the finding record and must not create a second classification or severity system.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 3 because a second taxonomy can distort how valid findings are interpreted. Frequency is 2 because the issue arises only in flows that enrich findings for presentation. Breadth is 3 because the concern could affect any review surface once findings are normalized. Hosted detectability is 2 because deciding whether metadata is merely presentational or semantically competing requires architectural context beyond the final review text. Evidence strength is 1 because the candidate has no corroborating source IDs or evidence entries. False-positive risk is 3 because some auxiliary fields can look classification-like while still being harmless display data. Redundancy is 2 because the concern overlaps broader no-reclassification safeguards even though the exact handoff rule is new.

assessments.title: Presentation is render-only
assessments.applicabilityRationale: Preserving frozen finding semantics through final presentation is within Hosted review-quality scope, but this candidate is framed as a renderer-layer contract rather than a concise model instruction.
assessments.summary: The no-reclassification principle is useful, but the candidate should be reconsidered as a smaller review-skill rule rather than adopted verbatim.
assessments.impactDescription: If presentation adds, removes, or reinterprets findings, developers receive a different review than the evidence-supported finding set.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: Existing Hosted evidence rules prevent unsupported repository claims, but no current rule specifically preserves finding semantics after the findings set is frozen.
assessments.proposedText: Final presentation may reformat the frozen review data, but it must not add, remove, merge, split, dismiss, or reinterpret findings, or change their severity, classification, evidence, or verdict semantics.
