assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 4 because semantic drift in final presentation can materially change the review a developer acts on. Frequency is 2 because this risk appears only in multi-stage flows with a separate presentation step. Breadth is 4 because any surface can be affected once findings are rendered. Hosted detectability is 2 because proving that a rendered finding was reinterpreted rather than merely reformatted often requires access to the frozen payload. Evidence strength is 2 because the rule is sensible and internally documented, but there is no stronger external support in the provided catalog materials. False-positive risk is 3 because acceptable rephrasing can be hard to distinguish from semantic change. Redundancy is 2 because the catalog already has broad evidence discipline, though not this exact post-freeze safeguard.

assessments.title: Presentation consumes the schema payload exactly
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a renderer input-contract and hard-stop rule about schema loading and EOF completeness, not a Hosted review rule about repository defects or finding classification.
assessments.summary: The candidate belongs to schema validation and runtime failure handling for presentation.
assessments.impactDescription: A violation would produce a partial or malformed rendered body, but it would not create an independently reviewable repository-content defect in the Hosted catalog.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The Hosted catalog does not encode renderer schema-loading behavior or prompt hard-stop requirements for missing contracts.
assessments.proposedText: Only render a normal review body from a payload that fully satisfies the presentation schema and loaded contract. If any required schema, contract, or skill input is unavailable to EOF, stop instead of inventing fields or emitting a partial review.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 2 because malformed rendering is disruptive but not a direct code-review semantic defect. Frequency is 2 because payload or load failures are possible but not constant. Breadth is 1 because the rule is limited to one renderer contract. Hosted detectability is 5 because missing required fields and partial output are usually obvious. Evidence strength is 1 because the candidate lacks supporting catalog evidence beyond the contract itself. False-positive risk is 3 because some schema evolution could change required fields without meaning the review quality declined. Redundancy is 3 because contract-loading behavior sits outside the scope of the current Hosted rules.

assessments.title: `changeDescription` must be a change-focused review title
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This controls the wording quality of a rendered review heading rather than an independently enforceable Hosted rule about code-review evidence or repository correctness.
assessments.summary: The candidate is presentation-title guidance for the final review body.
assessments.impactDescription: A weak heading can make the review less informative, but it does not alter the validity of the findings about the code change itself.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog does not regulate final review-title phrasing or heading metadata quality.
assessments.proposedText: Set `changeDescription` to a concise summary of what the reviewed change does. Do not use only a PR number, branch name, or generic placeholder when the run already established a more specific change description.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 1 because the rule affects usefulness of the heading, not substantive defect analysis. Frequency is 3 because every rendered review needs a title. Breadth is 1 because the rule applies only to one metadata field. Hosted detectability is 4 because generic titles and placeholders are easy to spot. Evidence strength is 1 because there is no additional catalog evidence supporting this as Hosted review guidance. False-positive risk is 3 because title quality is partly subjective when change summaries are sparse. Redundancy is 4 because the catalog already omits output-template copy rules entirely.

assessments.title: Section order and headings are fixed
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an exact final-body template contract about headings, preamble text, and code fences rather than a Hosted review rule about evidence-backed defects.
assessments.summary: The candidate is a renderer layout specification, not catalog review guidance.
assessments.impactDescription: Violations would change the shape of the markdown output, but they would not independently establish that Hosted reviewed the repository incorrectly.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No active Hosted rule prescribes exact review headings or section order because the catalog focuses on repository-review semantics, not final-body templating.
assessments.proposedText: Render the normal successful review body with the canonical headings exactly once and in contract order. Do not add preamble text, extra reader-visible sections, or surrounding code fences.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 1 because the main consequence is formatting drift. Frequency is 3 because headings appear in every successful rendered review. Breadth is 1 because the rule is limited to one output template. Hosted detectability is 5 because missing or reordered headings are easy to compare against the contract. Evidence strength is 1 because there is no broader catalog evidence for elevating template order into Hosted review guidance. False-positive risk is 2 because exact heading mismatches are objective. Redundancy is 4 because the catalog intentionally excludes presentation-template rules.

assessments.title: Canonical sample output block is the visual audit reference
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This candidate establishes how to read an illustrative sample and which authority wins when examples diverge; it is documentation for renderer auditing, not an independently enforceable Hosted review rule.
assessments.summary: The candidate is explanatory reference material around a sample block, not a Hosted rule candidate.
assessments.impactDescription: Its failure would create ambiguity in renderer documentation, but it would not directly change defect detection or finding classification in Hosted review output.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The Hosted catalog contains enforceable rules, not meta-guidance about illustrative examples or precedence between samples and schemas.
assessments.proposedText: Treat the canonical sample output as a visual reference only. When an example conflicts with explicit presentation rules or the input schema, follow the explicit rule text and substitute real payload values instead of literal placeholders.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 0 because the content is interpretive reference material rather than a direct review safeguard. Frequency is 1 because the sample matters only when someone audits the renderer against the example. Breadth is 1 because it affects a single documentation aid. Hosted detectability is 5 because example-versus-rule precedence is explicit on inspection. Evidence strength is 1 because no other catalog evidence elevates sample-reading guidance into a Hosted rule. False-positive risk is 5 because enforcing illustrative example guidance as a model rule would overread non-normative content. Redundancy is 5 because the candidate itself says explicit rules and schema already win.

assessments.title: Section bodies render from payload data only
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a section-by-section renderer contract about ordering, empty states, and list rendering, not a Hosted repository-review rule.
assessments.summary: The candidate specifies presentation-template behavior for section bodies rather than Hosted review semantics.
assessments.impactDescription: A violation would reorder or restyle rendered sections, but it would not independently prove the underlying review of the code change was wrong.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog does not constrain how a downstream renderer lays out section bodies, payload order, or empty bullets.
assessments.proposedText: Render each review section from the supplied payload data in payload order. Do not invent recommendations, reorder findings, or use anything other than a single `- None` bullet for an empty list-backed section.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 2 because section-body drift can obscure findings but usually does not create new defect claims. Frequency is 3 because these sections appear in normal review output. Breadth is 2 because multiple sections are affected, but only inside the presentation layer. Hosted detectability is 4 because reordered items and invented bullets are visible in output. Evidence strength is 1 because there is no supporting catalog evidence beyond the contract. False-positive risk is 3 because some section reshaping could still preserve meaning. Redundancy is 4 because the Hosted catalog deliberately leaves section rendering to downstream presentation logic.

assessments.title: `MUST FIX` is the linter-action section
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This governs the markdown shape of one renderer section and how linter items are displayed, not an independently enforceable Hosted review rule about repository defects.
assessments.summary: The candidate is section-specific presentation guidance for linter output.
assessments.impactDescription: Its failure would affect how linter actions are shown in the review body, but not whether Hosted correctly identifies code or test defects.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No active Hosted rule prescribes the display format of the `MUST FIX` section because the catalog does not own final-body section rendering.
assessments.proposedText: Render `MUST FIX` from the supplied `mustFix` entries as plain bullets in payload order. Reserve that section for actionable linter lines or the explicit `- None` empty state, and do not render finding cards there.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 1 because the rule affects display of linter follow-up, not core review correctness. Frequency is 2 because not every review includes a populated `MUST FIX` section. Breadth is 1 because the scope is one subsection. Hosted detectability is 4 because structured cards versus plain bullets are easy to spot. Evidence strength is 1 because only the internal contract supports the requirement here. False-positive risk is 2 because the display distinction is fairly objective. Redundancy is 3 because the current catalog intentionally omits renderer subsection rules.

assessments.title: Structured findings in issues and observations render as heading-based finding blocks
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a highly specific markdown rendering contract for structured finding cards, including labels, fences, and fallback rules, rather than a Hosted rule about review semantics.
assessments.summary: The candidate defines an exact finding-card output shape for the renderer.
assessments.impactDescription: A violation would produce the wrong card layout or fallback shape, but it would not by itself show that Hosted identified the wrong repository defect.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog does not regulate exact markdown card layouts, heading levels, or code-block placement for rendered findings.
assessments.proposedText: Non-empty `ISSUES` and `OBSERVATIONS` must render schema-complete structured findings in the canonical heading-plus-field-block format, with ordered `Impact`, `Evidence`, and optional `Suggested Change` lines and any payload-supplied code blocks. Do not fall back to plain strings for non-empty sections; if a finding is not presentation-complete, stop instead of inventing a fallback shape.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 2 because finding-card shape affects readability and downstream compatibility more than substantive review correctness. Frequency is 2 because structured cards appear only when rich finding objects are present. Breadth is 1 because the rule is confined to issues and observations rendering. Hosted detectability is 5 because exact heading, label, and code-block mismatches are easy to compare. Evidence strength is 1 because no upstream or maintainer evidence in the catalog elevates this layout contract into Hosted guidance. False-positive risk is 2 because the output shape is objective. Redundancy is 3 because the Hosted catalog does not currently own renderer markup conventions.

assessments.title: Presentation priority and review-type mappings remain active
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The candidate includes genuine cross-surface review taxonomy semantics, but it mixes those semantics with presentation emojis and output-label mappings that are too UI-specific for direct Hosted inclusion.
assessments.summary: Priority and review-type intent may warrant future Hosted guidance, but the current candidate overcouples taxonomy meaning to presentation-specific mappings.
assessments.impactDescription: Without a stable taxonomy, the same finding can be labeled inconsistently across review flows, but adopting UI-specific mappings would also make Hosted rules brittle.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no cross-surface rule defining review priority or review-type taxonomy, and no active rule depends on emoji or renderer labels.
assessments.proposedText: Use a stable review taxonomy: `change-request`, `nitpick`, `refactor-suggestion`, `thought-or-concern`, `positive-feedback`, and `future-consideration` define review intent, while `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low`, `observation`, `notable`, and `good` define priority or strength. Do not use positive-feedback priorities for issues, and keep observation and future-consideration classifications non-blocking.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 3 because unstable taxonomy can blur how strongly a developer should react to a finding. Frequency is 2 because many reviews can work without the richer taxonomy even when it is available. Breadth is 4 because a cross-surface taxonomy would apply everywhere once adopted. Hosted detectability is 2 because distinguishing semantic taxonomy drift from acceptable presentation variation needs more context than the final label alone. Evidence strength is 1 because the candidate is supported only by the internal presentation contract. False-positive risk is 4 because the candidate bundles semantic intent with display mappings, making over-enforcement likely. Redundancy is 2 because the catalog lacks this taxonomy today, but some of the intent overlaps broader evidence and classification discipline.

assessments.title: Shared output keeps the legacy explanatory sections
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This candidate preserves a mixed rendering mode for plain bullets and expanded cards, which is a renderer compatibility detail rather than a Hosted review rule.
assessments.summary: The candidate is about coexistence of two display shapes in a rendered section.
assessments.impactDescription: A violation would flatten or restyle findings in the final markdown, but it would not independently establish a repository-review defect.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The Hosted catalog does not constrain whether the renderer supports mixed legacy and expanded display forms in one section.
assessments.proposedText: When a section contains both plain-bullet findings and expanded finding cards, preserve each supplied item in its provided shape. Do not collapse a supplied finding card into a plain bullet just because the section also contains bullet items.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 1 because the consequence is mainly presentation compatibility. Frequency is 1 because mixed-mode sections are a narrower subset of rendered reviews. Breadth is 1 because the rule affects one display behavior. Hosted detectability is 4 because collapse from card to bullet is visible. Evidence strength is 1 because only the internal presentation contract supports this exact requirement. False-positive risk is 4 because different acceptable renderers could reasonably choose one consistent display form. Redundancy is 4 because the current Hosted catalog excludes display-shape compatibility rules.

assessments.title: File references must stay stable and non-local
assessments.applicabilityRationale: Stable, non-local file references are part of evidence quality in the emitted review body, and the failure mode is independently enforceable in Hosted output.
assessments.summary: The catalog lacks a rule that forbids editor-local or absolute-disk file references in review output.
assessments.impactDescription: Local URIs and machine paths can leak environment details and break the stable repository-scoped evidence links that developers need to act on a finding.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: Current Hosted rules assume repository evidence and file-based findings, but none constrain the shape of emitted file references or forbid local-path leakage in review text.
assessments.proposedText: Do not emit editor-local URIs or absolute disk paths in review output. Use repository-relative or authoritative PR-scoped file references only.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 4 because local-path leakage can expose environment details and undermine actionable evidence links. Frequency is 2 because file references are common, but outright local-link corruption is not expected on every review. Breadth is 3 because the safeguard applies across any review surface that cites files. Hosted detectability is 5 because forbidden URI and path prefixes are explicit and easy to check. Evidence strength is 2 because the rule is only backed by the internal presentation contract, but the failure mode is concrete and specific. False-positive risk is 1 because repository-relative references are usually easy to distinguish from editor-local or absolute-disk paths. Redundancy is 1 because no current Hosted rule covers this output-evidence safeguard.

assessments.title: Presentation is render-only and owns no review business logic
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The candidate's ban on presentation-owned classification logic is relevant to Hosted review fidelity, but the rule is a broad architecture restatement that overlaps other render-only candidates and lacks a clean standalone failure condition.
assessments.summary: The no-business-logic principle is directionally correct, but this candidate needs narrower wording before it becomes a Hosted rule.
assessments.impactDescription: If the presentation layer starts deciding issue versus observation placement or compensating for invalid payloads, final findings can drift away from the evidence-backed review result.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no explicit post-freeze business-logic rule, though its evidence rules already assume findings are not silently reinterpreted downstream.
assessments.proposedText: After findings are frozen, the presentation layer must render the supplied classifications, severities, recommendations, and verdicts without inventing, merging, suppressing, or reclassifying them. If the payload is invalid, stop instead of compensating with new review logic.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 3 because downstream business-logic drift can change how valid findings are presented to developers. Frequency is 2 because the issue appears only in architectures with a distinct presentation layer. Breadth is 4 because any surface could be affected once findings are routed through that layer. Hosted detectability is 2 because separating harmless formatting from illicit business logic often requires access to upstream payloads and renderer responsibilities. Evidence strength is 1 because the candidate has no corroborating evidence beyond the internal contract. False-positive risk is 3 because some presentational choices can look like classification logic without actually changing meaning. Redundancy is 3 because the candidate overlaps other render-only and no-reclassification concepts in this batch.

assessments.title: Linter execution report renders from structured payload fields
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an exact renderer contract for one subsection's field source and field order, not a Hosted rule about repository defects or evidence-based review findings.
assessments.summary: The candidate belongs to linter-report presentation, not the Hosted review catalog.
assessments.impactDescription: A violation would reorder or restyle the rendered linter execution report, but would not independently show that Hosted reviewed the code change incorrectly.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog does not prescribe how a rendered linter execution report is composed or ordered.
assessments.proposedText: Render the linter execution report from the structured `linterReport` fields in the contract order `Version`, `Status`, `Run Scope`, `Issue Count`, `Summary`. Use only the supplied `mustFix` entries for `MUST FIX`; do not derive actions from summary prose.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 1 because this is a subsection formatting and sourcing issue. Frequency is 2 because linter report rendering is common but not universal. Breadth is 1 because the scope is one report block. Hosted detectability is 4 because wrong field order or wrong field source is visible in output when the payload is known. Evidence strength is 1 because no broader catalog evidence supports promoting this renderer detail. False-positive risk is 2 because the exact order requirement is objective. Redundancy is 3 because the Hosted catalog does not currently own renderer report-shape rules.

assessments.title: Footer rendering is deterministic
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This controls footer presence, ordering, and suppression of ledger fields in the rendered body rather than an independently enforceable Hosted review rule about repository defects.
assessments.summary: The candidate is a presentation-footer contract, not Hosted review guidance.
assessments.impactDescription: Its failure would alter verification footer formatting, but it would not directly change the correctness of code-review findings.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The Hosted catalog does not regulate footer rendering, verification markers, or post-body text in review output.
assessments.proposedText: When the normal successful review path includes a verification footer, render it exactly once with `Preflight complete: yes` before the ordered `Skill used:` lines. Omit execution-ledger fields and `review-presentation`, and emit no trailing text after the footer.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 1 because the footer is ancillary to the substantive review. Frequency is 2 because the footer appears on normal successful rendered reviews but not every possible path. Breadth is 1 because the scope is one footer block. Hosted detectability is 5 because missing or extra footer lines are obvious. Evidence strength is 1 because only the internal presentation contract supports this requirement. False-positive risk is 2 because the footer expectations are explicit. Redundancy is 3 because the current Hosted catalog does not include footer-format rules.

assessments.title: Prompt and renderer authority stay separated
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an internal authority-boundary rule for prompts and the renderer, mixing workflow routing and display-semantics ownership rather than defining a standalone Hosted review rule.
assessments.summary: The candidate belongs to prompt-versus-renderer orchestration, not the current Hosted review catalog.
assessments.impactDescription: A violation would blur ownership between workflow stages, but it would not by itself define a repository defect or a reusable Hosted finding rule.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog does not define prompt authority, renderer authority, or successful-output-path ownership boundaries.
assessments.proposedText: Keep prompt and renderer responsibilities separate: prompts own routing, hard-stops, and whether the successful-output path is reached, while the renderer owns only the final successful review body after findings are frozen. Do not invent missing rich-display semantics in prompts or new workflow, scope, or verification logic in the renderer.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 2 because authority bleed can cause inconsistent output behavior, but it is still a pipeline concern more than a repository-review rule. Frequency is 2 because separate prompt and renderer roles are not present in every Hosted flow. Breadth is 2 because the rule spans multiple internal stages, though still inside one architecture. Hosted detectability is 3 because some authority violations are visible in output, but others require implementation knowledge. Evidence strength is 1 because no other provided catalog evidence supports elevating this orchestration split. False-positive risk is 4 because responsibility boundaries can shift legitimately as the system architecture evolves. Redundancy is 3 because the current Hosted catalog intentionally omits these pipeline ownership rules.

assessments.title: Overall assessment must preserve frozen verdict semantics
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is renderer and workflow-freeze behavior, not repository review guidance that the Hosted catalog can apply as an independently enforceable review rule.
assessments.summary: The candidate governs post-review rendering semantics rather than how Hosted review should evaluate code or write findings.
assessments.impactDescription: If this behavior is wrong, the review system can misrender a frozen verdict, but that is an orchestration defect outside the Hosted instruction catalog's repository-review scope.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog intentionally has no rule for renderer freeze semantics because it targets review guidance for repository changes, not output-pipeline behavior.
assessments.proposedText: Render the supplied `overallAssessment` without changing its verdict semantics. Do not rewrite the overall assessment to contradict the frozen `ISSUES` state.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 2 because contradictory rendering is undesirable but secondary to the underlying frozen findings; frequency 2 because it only matters when a review emits an overall assessment; breadth 1 because it affects presentation machinery rather than repository review; hostedDetectability 1 because the catalog cannot observe post-freeze renderer behavior; evidenceStrength 3 because the source rule is explicit; falsePositiveRisk 5 because enforcement would depend on internal workflow state the catalog does not model; redundancy 0 because no Hosted rule covers this area, and exclusion is still correct because the area is out of scope.

assessments.title: Skeptic pass augments, never replaces, the primary audit
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The candidate describes internal multi-pass review orchestration for a skeptic stage, not a standalone Hosted rule for evaluating repository changes or classifying findings.
assessments.summary: The source is mainly workflow machinery for when a skeptic pass runs and how it relates to a primary pass.
assessments.impactDescription: A bad skeptic-stage workflow could waste review effort or duplicate work, but that problem belongs to review orchestration rather than the Hosted repository-review catalog.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog has no skeptic-pass orchestration rules, which is appropriate because the catalog does not model internal pass scheduling or frozen-output timing.
assessments.proposedText: Use the skeptic pass only to add net-new issues or observations before output is frozen. Do not restate or replace the primary audit, and skip the skeptic pass entirely when the change set is empty or out of scope.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 2 because duplicate or misplaced skeptic processing is mostly workflow inefficiency; frequency 3 because a skeptic pass could run often in that workflow; breadth 1 because it affects internal review staging rather than repository surfaces; hostedDetectability 1 because the catalog cannot tell whether a secondary pass ran before freeze or skipped for scope; evidenceStrength 3 because the contract text is clear; falsePositiveRisk 4 because translating stage-control rules into review guidance would overfire; redundancy 1 because only the anti-duplication idea overlaps with broader review concerns, while the candidate as written is still out of scope.

assessments.title: Skeptic proposes findings only from evidence
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The core requirement is an enforceable Hosted review skill: issues need concrete evidence, unsupported concerns must be downgraded or omitted, and assumptions must be labeled.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted catalog lacks a direct rule requiring concrete evidence for issues and explicit labeling of assumptions in review findings.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this rule, Hosted review can overstate speculative concerns as issues, reducing trust in findings across all surfaces.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No current Hosted rule directly governs reviewer evidence thresholds, assumption labeling, or when weakly supported concerns must be demoted from issue severity.
assessments.proposedText: Raise an issue only when concrete evidence supports it, such as a file:line reference, quoted code, tool output, or a demonstrable matching pattern elsewhere in the repository. If a concern depends on inference, label the assumption explicitly and downgrade it to an observation or omit it unless stronger evidence exists.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 5 because unsupported issues directly damage review trust; frequency 4 because most substantive reviews rely on evidence-based findings; breadth 5 because the rule applies across implementation, testing, and documentation review; hostedDetectability 4 because missing evidence and unlabeled assumptions are usually visible in the finding text; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate states a clear hierarchy that matches common review expectations; falsePositiveRisk 2 because citations and explicit assumptions are concrete and reviewable; redundancy 1 because the current Hosted catalog has no comparable review-evidence rule, so adding one is justified.

assessments.title: Adversarial attack surface is explicit
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The candidate contributes a reusable Hosted review-skill rule: reviewers should check common failure classes and stay within loaded repository guidance instead of inventing unsupported policy.
assessments.summary: The Hosted catalog lacks an explicit cross-cutting reviewer checklist for common defect classes and unsupported-policy avoidance.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this guidance, Hosted review can miss whole categories of defects or assert requirements that the loaded repository guidance does not support.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: Current Hosted implementation and testing rules encode many domain-specific defects, but no rule tells the reviewer to systematically cover major failure classes or avoid inventing policy beyond loaded guidance.
assessments.proposedText: When reviewing substantive changes, consider at least correctness or logic errors, error handling and nil or zero-value paths, concurrency or ordering, input validation and trust boundaries, resource lifecycle or residual state, security exposure, and missing tests for behavior-changing branches. Apply loaded repository guidance for service-specific patterns and do not invent unsupported policy.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because blind spots across these defect classes can hide meaningful regressions; frequency 4 because every substantive code review benefits from this checklist; breadth 5 because it spans implementation defects and associated testing gaps; hostedDetectability 2 because reviewer completeness is harder to observe than a single syntax rule; evidenceStrength 3 because the contract is clear but partly framed as reviewer process; falsePositiveRisk 3 because the checklist needs judgment and could overfire if phrased too rigidly; redundancy 1 because no current Hosted rule provides this cross-cutting review-skill guidance.

assessments.title: Issues must name a concrete failure scenario
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a directly enforceable review-classification rule: issue-level findings should explain the concrete failure path and otherwise stay at observation severity.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted catalog does not explicitly require issue findings to tie evidence to an observable failure scenario.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this rule, Hosted review can file vague issue-level findings that do not explain what breaks, making prioritization and validation harder.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No current Hosted rule governs the distinction between a concrete issue and a weaker observation based on whether the finding explains an observable failure, regression, policy violation, or missing requirement.
assessments.proposedText: Raise an issue only when the evidence supports a concrete failure path, regression, policy violation, or missing required behavior. If the concern cannot explain an observable failure, keep it as an observation instead of an issue.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 5 because vague issue findings distort verdicts and reviewer trust; frequency 4 because many potential comments need issue-versus-observation classification; breadth 5 because the standard applies to all review surfaces; hostedDetectability 4 because the presence or absence of a failure explanation is usually visible in the finding text; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate gives a crisp and reviewable threshold; falsePositiveRisk 2 because the rule asks for an observable failure path rather than subjective polish; redundancy 1 because the Hosted catalog currently lacks this classification rule.

assessments.title: Skeptic does not finalize outcomes
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The candidate governs internal moderation and freeze mechanics for a skeptic stage, not repository-review guidance that belongs in the Hosted catalog.
assessments.summary: The source is about who can finalize wording and visibility inside a review workflow, not about evaluating code changes.
assessments.impactDescription: If this workflow rule is violated, moderation behavior can be wrong, but the defect is in review orchestration rather than the Hosted rule catalog.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog appropriately omits moderation-freeze rules because it focuses on repository review behavior, not internal review pipeline control.
assessments.proposedText: The skeptic pass may propose findings, but moderation owns final wording and visibility before output is frozen. Do not mark skeptic findings as final or immune from moderation.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 2 because incorrect moderation ownership is a workflow problem more than a repository-review failure; frequency 2 because it only matters when an internal skeptic stage exists; breadth 1 because it does not map to implementation, testing, or documentation surfaces; hostedDetectability 1 because the catalog cannot inspect moderation state; evidenceStrength 3 because the candidate is explicit; falsePositiveRisk 5 because any attempted Hosted enforcement would speculate about invisible workflow mechanics; redundancy 0 because no current Hosted rule covers this orchestration layer and exclusion is appropriate.

assessments.title: No duplicate or redundant candidates
assessments.applicabilityRationale: Avoiding duplicate findings is an enforceable review-output quality rule that can be applied independent of the skeptic-pass framing.
assessments.summary: The Hosted catalog lacks a direct rule to merge duplicated concerns and attach new evidence to an existing finding instead of inflating the count.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this rule, Hosted review can overcount the same defect, making the review noisier and less actionable.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No current Hosted rule tells the reviewer to consolidate duplicate concerns and add net-new evidence to an existing finding rather than emitting another finding.
assessments.proposedText: Do not emit duplicate findings for the same underlying concern. Add new evidence to the existing finding instead of restating it, and open a separate finding only when the change introduces a distinct defect.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 3 because duplication hurts clarity more than correctness; frequency 4 because overlapping concerns are common in broad reviews; breadth 5 because the rule applies to all review surfaces; hostedDetectability 4 because duplicated findings are usually evident from their text and evidence; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate is concrete and operational; falsePositiveRisk 1 because distinct-versus-duplicate concerns can usually be judged from the finding scope; redundancy 1 because the current Hosted catalog has no direct anti-duplication rule.

assessments.title: One concern, one classification
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a clear review-classification rule: a single concern should not appear in multiple severity buckets, and uncertain severity should default to the lower justified classification.
assessments.summary: The Hosted catalog lacks a direct rule preventing the same concern from appearing as both an issue and an observation.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this rule, Hosted review can present inconsistent severity for the same concern and confuse the overall verdict.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No current Hosted rule governs mutually exclusive finding classification or the lower-justified fallback when severity is uncertain.
assessments.proposedText: Do not classify the same concern as both an issue and an observation. When severity is uncertain, use the lower justified classification until stronger evidence supports escalation.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because conflicting classification directly affects verdict quality; frequency 3 because not every review has borderline severity calls, but many do; breadth 5 because the rule applies across all review domains; hostedDetectability 4 because duplicate cross-bucket concerns are visible in the output; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate gives a precise classification rule; falsePositiveRisk 2 because the lower-justified fallback is concrete and conservative; redundancy 1 because the current Hosted catalog does not cover this classification behavior.

assessments.title: The skeptic pass produces no separate output section
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This candidate controls how an internal skeptic stage is rendered in the final review body, which is presentation and workflow behavior outside the Hosted repository-review catalog.
assessments.summary: The source is about suppressing skeptic-pass headings, labels, and narration rather than reviewing repository changes.
assessments.impactDescription: If violated, the final review format may expose internal process details, but that is an output-presentation concern rather than a Hosted review rule for code changes.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog intentionally has no rule for internal-pass section rendering because its scope is repository review guidance, not output formatting for hidden workflow stages.
assessments.proposedText: The skeptic pass must not produce its own rendered section, heading, or process narration. Findings that survive moderation should appear only as ordinary issues or observations without skeptic-specific labeling.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 1 because this is mainly formatting of internal workflow output; frequency 3 because a skeptic pass could appear often if the workflow uses one; breadth 1 because it affects presentation rather than repository surfaces; hostedDetectability 2 because headings and labels are visible but the hidden-stage intent is not; evidenceStrength 3 because the source text is clear; falsePositiveRisk 4 because enforcing hidden-stage presentation in Hosted guidance would couple to workflow details; redundancy 0 because no current Hosted rule covers this and exclusion remains appropriate.

assessments.title: Do not invent acceptance patterns
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an enforceable acceptance-test review rule and the active Hosted testing rule already captures the same requirement.
assessments.summary: The candidate is already covered by the active Hosted rule that requires following the nearest same-service acceptance pattern and avoiding unnecessary new local patterns.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this guard, test contributions can drift into inconsistent helper, assertion, naming, and scenario conventions that make maintenance harder.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-EVID-001 already says to follow the nearest same-service acceptance pattern for naming, configuration helpers, assertions, and scenario shape, and to flag a new local pattern when an established provider pattern already covers the scenario.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because unnecessary pattern drift degrades test consistency; frequency 4 because contributors routinely copy or extend nearby tests; breadth 4 because the rule affects multiple dimensions of acceptance-test structure; hostedDetectability 4 because divergent local patterns are usually visible in changed test code; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate and active Hosted rule are semantically aligned; falsePositiveRisk 1 because comparisons to nearby same-service tests are concrete; redundancy 5 because TEST-EVID-001 already fully covers the requirement, so no catalog change is needed.
assessments.proposedText: Follow the nearest same-service acceptance pattern for naming, configuration helpers, assertions, and scenario shape. Flag a new local pattern only when an established provider pattern covers the same scenario.

assessments.title: Basic acceptance tests should prove existence
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a direct acceptance-test assertion rule and the current Hosted rule already matches it semantically.
assessments.summary: The candidate is already covered by the active Hosted rule requiring a basic managed-resource test to prove existence in Azure.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this guard, basic tests can pass without proving that the resource was actually created in Azure.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-PATTERN-001 already requires a basic managed-resource test to prove the object exists in Azure, normally with `check.That(data.ResourceName).ExistsInAzure(r)`.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because existence proof is foundational to a basic resource test; frequency 4 because most resource test suites include a basic scenario; breadth 3 because it is scoped to basic managed-resource tests; hostedDetectability 4 because missing existence checks are usually easy to spot in the test body; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate and active rule say the same thing; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the expectation is precise; redundancy 5 because TEST-PATTERN-001 already fully covers the rule.
assessments.proposedText: A basic managed-resource test must prove the object exists in Azure, normally with `check.That(data.ResourceName).ExistsInAzure(r)`.

assessments.title: Prefer ImportStep for broad validation
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The candidate is an enforceable testing rule and its meaning already matches the active Hosted rule on `ImportStep()` and extra assertions.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted rule already captures the preference for `data.ImportStep()` as broad post-create validation and limits extra assertions to behavior import cannot prove.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this guard, tests can accumulate brittle field assertions where the import step would already validate state more broadly.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-PATTERN-002 already says to prefer `data.ImportStep()` for broad post-create state validation and to add field assertions only for computed or edge behavior that import cannot prove.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 3 because the rule is mainly about robust test shape rather than a catastrophic defect; frequency 4 because import validation is common in managed-resource tests; breadth 3 because it affects post-create validation design; hostedDetectability 4 because use of `ImportStep()` and extra assertions is visible in the test steps; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate and Hosted rule are semantically identical; falsePositiveRisk 2 because some scenarios genuinely need extra assertions but the rule already allows that; redundancy 5 because TEST-PATTERN-002 already covers the requirement completely.
assessments.proposedText: Prefer `data.ImportStep()` for broad post-create state validation. Add field assertions only for computed or edge behavior that import cannot prove.

assessments.title: Complete tests should cover the full supported shape when needed
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The candidate refines an existing Hosted lifecycle-matrix rule by defining what `complete` coverage must prove and when narrower targeted cases do not satisfy it.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted lifecycle rule requires `complete` coverage but does not yet explain when a distinct `complete` scenario is required for broader supported shapes.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this clarification, Hosted review can accept targeted niche tests as substitutes for a missing broad `complete` scenario, leaving optional blocks or broader supported configurations unexercised.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-WF-002 already requires `basic`, `requiresImport`, `complete`, `update`, and `ImportStep()` coverage when supported, but it does not define when a resource still needs a distinct `complete` scenario beyond narrower targeted tests.
assessments.proposedText: Resource acceptance coverage should include `basic`, `requiresImport`, `complete`, and `update`, plus `ImportStep()` when import is supported. The `complete` scenario should exercise the broader supported configuration surface and is not satisfied by narrower targeted cases alone. When a resource exposes optional metadata, optional blocks, or multiple supported shapes beyond the narrow success path, include a distinct `complete` test unless concrete evidence shows that scenario is not applicable. Omission of any default scenario requires concrete evidence that it is not applicable.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because missing broad-shape coverage can hide lifecycle regressions; frequency 4 because many new resources expose optional blocks or wider supported shapes; breadth 4 because the clarification affects the default resource test matrix across services; hostedDetectability 3 because reviewers can usually tell when only narrow scenarios exist, though applicability still needs judgment; evidenceStrength 3 because the candidate is a local safeguard rather than a direct upstream wording match; falsePositiveRisk 2 because the rule keeps an evidence-based exception path; redundancy 2 because TEST-WF-002 partially covers the topic already, so the right action is to update rather than add a separate rule.

assessments.title: RequiresImport coverage is part of the default resource test matrix
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an enforceable acceptance-test lifecycle rule and the active Hosted testing catalog already covers it directly.
assessments.summary: The candidate is already covered by the active Hosted rule requiring default `requiresImport` coverage with evidence-based omission only when not applicable.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this guard, resource tests can miss import-collision behavior that is part of the default provider resource matrix.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-PATTERN-004 already requires dedicated `requiresImport` coverage by default, normally through `data.RequiresImportErrorStep`, and TEST-WF-002 also keeps `requiresImport` in the default matrix.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because missing import-collision coverage can leave a standard lifecycle branch untested; frequency 4 because most managed resources should consider it; breadth 4 because it is part of the shared resource test matrix; hostedDetectability 4 because presence or absence of `requiresImport` steps is visible in the tests; evidenceStrength 5 because the candidate is directly backed by upstream contributor guidance and matches the Hosted rule; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the rule already allows evidence-based exceptions; redundancy 5 because TEST-PATTERN-004 already captures the requirement exactly.
assessments.proposedText: Managed resources require dedicated `requiresImport` coverage by default, normally through `data.RequiresImportErrorStep`; omission requires evidence that import collision behavior is not applicable.

assessments.title: Do not add acctests for simple property validation when unit tests already cover it
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The candidate is an enforceable testing-scope rule and the active Hosted rule already expresses the same acceptance-versus-unit-test boundary.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted rule already says not to add acceptance tests solely for simple property validation already covered by unit tests.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this guard, acceptance suites can grow with slow, low-value tests that duplicate validator behavior already proven in unit coverage.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-PATTERN-005 already says not to add an acceptance test solely for simple property validation already covered by a unit test, and to reserve acceptance coverage for lifecycle, Azure runtime, or provider behavior beyond the validator.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 3 because the rule is about keeping acceptance scope efficient rather than preventing every defect; frequency 3 because validator-only scenarios appear regularly but not everywhere; breadth 3 because it affects a specific class of test additions; hostedDetectability 3 because reviewers need to compare the acceptance scenario against existing unit coverage; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate has explicit maintainer support and matches the Hosted rule; falsePositiveRisk 2 because the rule already allows acceptance tests when they prove broader behavior; redundancy 5 because TEST-PATTERN-005 already fully covers this guidance.
assessments.proposedText: Do not add an acceptance test solely for simple property validation already covered by a unit test; require acceptance coverage only for lifecycle, Azure runtime, or provider behavior beyond the validator.

assessments.title: Add acctests for CustomizeDiff logic so validation behavior is not left untested
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The candidate is an enforceable acceptance-test rule and the active Hosted rule already captures its substantive requirement.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted rule already requires targeted acceptance coverage for invalid `CustomizeDiff` paths and allows broader lifecycle scenarios to cover valid paths unless more assertions are needed.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this guard, regression-prone diff-time validation logic can be left untested or tested only through overly broad success scenarios.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-PATTERN-006 already says that `CustomizeDiff` constraints need targeted acceptance coverage for invalid paths, normally with `ExpectError`, while broader lifecycle scenarios can cover valid paths unless additional assertions are necessary.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because missing `CustomizeDiff` coverage can hide invalid-config regressions; frequency 3 because only some resources use this pattern; breadth 3 because it applies to a specific validation mechanism; hostedDetectability 4 because targeted `ExpectError` coverage is usually visible in test changes; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate and Hosted rule are semantically aligned; falsePositiveRisk 2 because the rule still permits broader valid-path coverage without overprescribing; redundancy 5 because TEST-PATTERN-006 already covers the requirement.
assessments.proposedText: `CustomizeDiff` constraints need targeted acceptance coverage for invalid paths, normally with `ExpectError`; broader lifecycle scenarios can cover valid paths unless additional assertions are necessary.

assessments.title: Inline one-use helper arguments in fmt.Sprintf-based config builders
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a narrow readability preference rather than a defect-oriented, broadly actionable Hosted review rule.
assessments.summary: The candidate encodes a localized style preference for single-use locals in test config builders, not a high-signal Hosted review safeguard.
assessments.impactDescription: Enforcing this as Hosted guidance would spend limited catalog budget on a readability nit that rarely changes correctness or test behavior.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog appropriately omits this style preference and focuses testing rules on lifecycle coverage, assertions, generated content, and Azure-specific harness behavior.
assessments.proposedText: In acceptance-test helpers that build configuration with `fmt.Sprintf(...)`, inline one-use helper results directly in the `fmt.Sprintf(...)` call. Keep a local only when the helper result is reused, transformed, or materially improves readability.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 1 because inline-versus-local helper style is low impact; frequency 3 because the pattern can recur in new test helpers; breadth 2 because it is confined to a narrow `fmt.Sprintf(...)` builder shape; hostedDetectability 5 because single-use locals are syntactically easy to spot; evidenceStrength 4 because the maintainer comment is direct; falsePositiveRisk 4 because reuse and readability exceptions are common and subjective; redundancy 1 because no current Hosted rule covers this nit, and the low impact means exclusion is better than adding more catalog surface.

assessments.title: Acctest helper struct names must stay canonical across all test variants
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The candidate meaningfully extends the active Hosted generated-test naming rule with established-versus-new surface guidance and explicit generator alignment.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted rule covers canonical helper reuse and generated-test drift, but it does not yet spell out how to preserve established names or choose generator-aligned names for new surfaces.
assessments.impactDescription: Without the added precision, Hosted review can miss casing or naming drift that only appears when generated identity tests or `go generate` disagree with handwritten helper types.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-PATTERN-008 already requires one canonical helper type across main, list, identity, and generated tests and forbids hand-editing generated identity tests or bridging drift with aliases or wrappers, but it lacks explicit guidance for existing canonical names versus new generator-aligned names.
assessments.proposedText: Use one canonical helper type per Terraform resource or data source across all handwritten and generated acceptance tests. Preserve an established helper type for existing surfaces; for new surfaces, choose the generator-aligned `ToCamel(<terraform-name>)Resource` or `ToCamel(<terraform-name>)DataSource` form and verify generated identity tests use the same name. Resolve mismatches by aligning the canonical helper type or intentionally changing the shared generator; do not hand-edit generated identity tests or bridge naming drift with aliases or wrappers.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because helper-name drift can break generation checks and leave the suite unstable; frequency 3 because the problem appears mainly on surfaces with generated identity coverage or multiple test variants; breadth 3 because it is limited to acceptance-test helper naming; hostedDetectability 4 because inconsistent helper types and generated diffs are usually visible in the changed files; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate is backed by specific upstream and local failure modes; falsePositiveRisk 2 because the established-versus-new surface split keeps the rule concrete; redundancy 2 because the active Hosted rule partially covers the topic already, so an update is better than a new rule.

assessments.title: Data source tests should prefer the associated resource complete config by default
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a scenario-dependent authoring heuristic with many valid exceptions, not a stable defect-oriented Hosted review rule.
assessments.summary: The candidate proposes a default preference for data-source setup shape, but the rule is too contextual to be a reliable Hosted safeguard.
assessments.impactDescription: Adding this would push Hosted review toward low-confidence style advice about test setup choices instead of higher-signal lifecycle and assertion defects.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog appropriately does not prescribe a single default setup helper for data source tests and instead focuses on lifecycle coverage, assertions, and established provider patterns.
assessments.proposedText: When a data source acceptance test needs managed-resource setup and the associated resource offers `complete(data)`, prefer that helper as the default setup shape. Use `basic(data)` or another narrower helper only when `complete(data)` is unavailable or the scenario intentionally needs less setup or less coupling.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 2 because the setup choice usually affects readability and convenience more than correctness; frequency 3 because data source tests often need managed-resource setup; breadth 2 because the rule only applies to one testing niche; hostedDetectability 2 because the best setup shape depends on scenario intent and surrounding helpers; evidenceStrength 2 because the candidate is inferred and explicitly preserves broad exceptions; falsePositiveRisk 5 because many legitimate tests should stay narrow or avoid `complete(data)`; redundancy 1 because no current Hosted rule covers this heuristic and the high ambiguity makes exclusion preferable.

assessments.title: Embedded Terraform in acceptance tests must use repository-valid indentation
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a concrete, enforceable acceptance-test formatting rule and the active Hosted testing rule already matches it.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted rule already requires two-space indentation and no tabs inside embedded Terraform configuration strings.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this guard, acceptance tests can fail repository formatting checks even when the Go code itself looks valid.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-PATTERN-010 already says embedded Terraform configuration must use two-space indentation and no tabs, and notes that Go formatting and Go tests do not detect invalid indentation inside raw strings.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 3 because bad heredoc indentation causes real CI failures but is usually localized; frequency 3 because embedded Terraform appears often enough in acceptance tests; breadth 2 because the rule is confined to raw Terraform strings; hostedDetectability 5 because tabs and indentation style are easy to inspect; evidenceStrength 4 because the candidate aligns with documented failure analysis and the Hosted rule; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the formatting expectation is precise; redundancy 5 because TEST-PATTERN-010 already fully captures the requirement.
assessments.proposedText: Embedded Terraform configuration must use two-space indentation and no tabs. Go formatting and Go tests do not detect invalid indentation inside raw strings.

assessments.title: Provider feature-flagged CRUD branch coverage
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a concrete acceptance-test review rule about how to cover provider feature branches and how to set up pre-existing Azure state.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted rule already captures the non-default feature branch scenario, the preference for one focused case, and the callback-based setup requirement.
assessments.impactDescription: Keeping the current wording preserves review coverage for feature-flagged CRUD branches without expanding the rule beyond its existing failure condition.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-PATTERN-011 already covers provider features that change CRUD, import, overwrite, or destroy behavior, requires one focused non-default scenario when feasible, and prefers `CheckWithClient...` setup over a second Terraform resource targeting the same remote ID.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 4 because missing feature-flag branch coverage can hide create, update, import, or destroy defects; frequency is 2 because only some provider features alter CRUD semantics; breadth is 3 because the pattern applies across multiple resources when such a feature exists; hostedDetectability is 4 because reviewers can inspect the scenario shape and setup helpers directly in test diffs; evidenceStrength is 4 because the candidate cites concrete harness behavior and Azure setup patterns; falsePositiveRisk is 1 because the trigger condition is narrow and specific; redundancy is 5 because the current TEST-PATTERN-011 already covers the same actionable failure condition, so no catalog change is needed.
assessments.proposedText: When a provider feature changes CRUD, import, overwrite, or destroy behavior, add one focused acceptance scenario for the non-default branch when feasible. Prepare pre-existing remote state with the appropriate `CheckWithClient...` helper instead of a second Terraform resource targeting the same ID.

assessments.title: Callback-based Azure pollers need explicit deadlines in acceptance setup helpers
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an acceptance-test harness rule for Azure polling inside callback-based setup helpers, which is directly reviewable in test code.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted rule already requires wrapping callback contexts with explicit deadlines before Azure polling and already distinguishes quota failures from missing deadlines.
assessments.impactDescription: Keeping the current rule retains the important deadline safeguard while avoiding a longer restatement of poller examples and common timeout ranges.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-PATTERN-012 already says that `CheckWithClientForResource`, `CheckWithClientWithoutResource`, and `CheckWithClient` callbacks must wrap their callback context with `context.WithTimeout(...)` or `context.WithDeadline(...)` before Azure polling, use an operation-appropriate deadline, and not misclassify quota failures as deadline issues.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 4 because missing deadlines can make acceptance setup fail consistently; frequency is 2 because only callback helpers that call Azure pollers are affected; breadth is 2 because the pattern is narrow but reusable across services; hostedDetectability is 4 because the callback context and poller calls are visible in diffs; evidenceStrength is 5 because the candidate cites the exact failure mode and concrete upstream fixes; falsePositiveRisk is 1 because the condition is precise; redundancy is 5 because TEST-PATTERN-012 already covers the same enforceable requirement, so the catalog should stay unchanged.
assessments.proposedText: When a `CheckWithClientForResource`, `CheckWithClientWithoutResource`, or `CheckWithClient` callback invokes an Azure polling helper, wrap its callback context with `context.WithTimeout(...)` or `context.WithDeadline(...)` before polling. Use an operation-appropriate deadline and do not confuse quota failures with missing deadlines.

assessments.title: Treat acceptance tests as real Azure activity
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is reviewer operating guidance about what test commands to suggest, not an independently enforceable defect rule for changed repository content.
assessments.summary: The candidate is useful general advice, but it does not map to a file-based Hosted review rule.
assessments.impactDescription: Excluding it keeps the Hosted catalog focused on repository-reviewable defects instead of conversational guidance about how broadly a reviewer should run tests.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The current Hosted catalog is scoped to implementation, testing, and documentation defects in changed files and does not define a rule for reviewer test-run recommendations.
assessments.proposedText: Treat acceptance tests as real Azure activity that can create billable resources. Prefer the narrowest `-run` scope that validates the change and avoid recommending full-suite runs when a targeted acceptance run is sufficient.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 1 because overbroad run suggestions mainly waste time and cost rather than introducing a repository defect; frequency is 3 because reviewers often discuss how to validate acceptance-test changes; breadth is 2 because the advice applies only to validation guidance around Azure acceptance runs; hostedDetectability is 0 because the Hosted catalog is attached to changed repository content, not free-form reviewer run recommendations; evidenceStrength is 1 because the candidate provides no sourced evidence; falsePositiveRisk is 4 because a generic bias against broader runs would be highly context-sensitive; redundancy is 1 because the current catalog does not already encode this advice, but the lack of repository-level enforceability supports exclusion.

assessments.title: Prefer narrow, scenario-focused test updates
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a testing-review concept about redundant or overbroad acceptance coverage, which is within Hosted testing scope.
assessments.summary: The actionable parts of this candidate are already covered by narrower Hosted testing rules, and the remaining smallest-set phrasing is too subjective for a separate rule.
assessments.impactDescription: Not adding a general minimization rule preserves required lifecycle coverage while still letting existing concrete rules reject redundant or mis-scoped tests.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-WF-002 defines the default lifecycle matrix, TEST-PATTERN-004 covers `requiresImport`, TEST-PATTERN-005 rejects acceptance tests that only duplicate unit validation, and TEST-PATTERN-011 already prefers one focused feature-branch scenario instead of multiplying equivalent cases.
assessments.proposedText: Add only the acceptance-test scenarios needed to prove the changed behavior. Do not add scenarios that only duplicate existing `basic`, `requiresImport`, `complete`, `update`, `ImportStep()`, import, or focused non-default feature-branch coverage.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 2 because over-testing mainly costs time and Azure resources rather than causing functional defects; frequency is 3 because many acceptance-test diffs could expand scenario count; breadth is 4 because the idea could reach most resource test suites; hostedDetectability is 2 because deciding the smallest sufficient set is subjective from a diff alone; evidenceStrength is 1 because no concrete source or repository pattern is cited; falsePositiveRisk is 4 because a broad minimization rule could suppress legitimately distinct coverage; redundancy is 4 because the current Hosted catalog already covers the concrete redundant-test cases, which supports keeping the catalog unchanged.

assessments.title: Resource acceptance tests should cover the core lifecycle by default
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a core acceptance-test lifecycle rule with a clear default matrix and a clear omission standard.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted rule already states the same default lifecycle matrix and the same requirement for concrete evidence before omitting a scenario.
assessments.impactDescription: Keeping the current wording preserves a high-value, easy-to-enforce lifecycle coverage rule without changing its meaning.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-WF-002 already requires `basic`, `requiresImport`, `complete`, `update`, and `ImportStep()` coverage when supported, and it already says omissions need concrete evidence that a scenario is not applicable.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 5 because missing core lifecycle coverage can hide major resource defects; frequency is 4 because this expectation applies to a large share of resource acceptance work; breadth is 5 because it spans most managed resources; hostedDetectability is 5 because reviewers can directly inspect the scenario matrix in test diffs; evidenceStrength is 5 because the candidate cites multiple upstream contributor guides; falsePositiveRisk is 1 because the expected scenarios and omission exception are explicit; redundancy is 5 because TEST-WF-002 already captures the same rule completely, so no update is needed.
assessments.proposedText: Resource acceptance coverage should include `basic`, `requiresImport`, `complete`, `update`, and `ImportStep()` when supported. Omission requires concrete evidence that a scenario is not applicable.

assessments.title: Use resource-specific `preCheck` helpers for optional prerequisites
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is an acceptance-test structure rule about optional prerequisites, skip behavior, and local helper placement.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted rule already captures the enforceable `preCheck` behaviors, and the extra closeness-to-tests guidance does not justify a catalog change.
assessments.impactDescription: Keeping the current rule preserves the important skip-versus-fail and no-duplicate-global-check safeguards without turning stylistic helper placement advice into a Hosted requirement.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-WF-002A already requires a receiver `preCheck(t *testing.T)` for optional prerequisites beyond global Azure checks, requires missing optional prerequisites to skip rather than fail, and forbids duplicating the framework's global Azure-auth checks.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 3 because wrong pre-check behavior can cause avoidable acceptance failures or brittle tests; frequency is 3 because optional prerequisites recur in some services; breadth is 3 because the pattern applies across multiple resource suites with special setup; hostedDetectability is 4 because helper names, call sites, and skip-versus-fail behavior are visible in diffs; evidenceStrength is 4 because the candidate cites upstream contributor guidance; falsePositiveRisk is 2 because the main rule is specific, though exact helper placement is somewhat stylistic; redundancy is 4 because the current TEST-WF-002A already contains the enforceable parts, so no update is warranted.
assessments.proposedText: Optional prerequisites beyond global Azure authentication and locations belong in a receiver `preCheck(t *testing.T)` called by each affected test. Missing optional prerequisites should skip, not fail, and global checks must not be duplicated.

assessments.title: New resources with list resources should include list query coverage
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a concrete testing rule for list-resource coverage tied to a specific upstream query-test pattern.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted rule already captures the Terraform 1.14 list-query coverage requirement, the multiple-resource setup, the narrowed-query expectation, and the approved-exception path.
assessments.impactDescription: Keeping the current rule preserves the enforceable list-resource coverage requirement without rewording an already accurate compact rule.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-WF-003 already requires new list resources to have Terraform 1.14 query coverage that provisions multiple resources and exercises the base query plus a narrowed query when supported, unless the list resource has an approved exception.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 3 because missing list-query coverage can leave a new list resource unvalidated; frequency is 2 because list resources are a subset of new resource work; breadth is 2 because the pattern applies narrowly to list resources; hostedDetectability is 4 because reviewers can inspect whether the required query scenarios exist; evidenceStrength is 4 because the candidate cites upstream list-resource guidance; falsePositiveRisk is 2 because the rule is specific but exception handling requires some context; redundancy is 5 because TEST-WF-003 already covers the same enforceable requirement fully.
assessments.proposedText: A new list resource should have Terraform 1.14 query coverage that provisions multiple resources and exercises the base query plus a narrowed query when supported, unless the list resource has an approved exception.

assessments.title: Ephemeral resource tests should use the framework ephemeral test pattern
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a test-pattern rule for provider ephemeral resources and their framework-specific acceptance harness.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted rule already covers the enforceable ephemeral-test pattern, including Terraform 1.10 gating, framework provider factories, and `echo` provider payload validation.
assessments.impactDescription: Keeping the current wording retains the key harness safeguards while leaving exact filename and helper-call details as implementation pattern specifics rather than separate Hosted requirements.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-WF-004 already requires the service-local framework ephemeral pattern, Terraform 1.10 gating, framework provider factories, and use of the `echo` provider when validating ephemeral result payloads.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 3 because the wrong ephemeral harness can invalidate test coverage; frequency is 1 because ephemeral resources are uncommon; breadth is 1 because the rule applies to a very narrow test surface; hostedDetectability is 4 because the file shape, gating, and harness choices are directly visible in diffs; evidenceStrength is 3 because the rule is inferred from concrete upstream tests rather than a published contributor document; falsePositiveRisk is 2 because the pattern is specific but exact helper spelling is less important than the harness behavior; redundancy is 4 because the current TEST-WF-004 already captures the enforceable rule and the candidate mostly adds lower-level pattern detail.
assessments.proposedText: Ephemeral resource tests should use the service-local framework pattern, Terraform 1.10 gating, framework provider factories, and the `echo` provider when validating result payloads.

assessments.title: Provider-defined functions should use focused framework unit tests
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a concrete testing rule for provider-defined function coverage, harness selection, and Terraform version gating.
assessments.summary: The current Hosted rule covers location, Terraform 1.8 gating, and output assertions, but it should explicitly require the `resource.UnitTest` harness with framework provider factories.
assessments.impactDescription: This update closes a specificity gap so reviewers can consistently flag provider-defined function tests that use the wrong harness or omit the framework provider factories.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: TEST-WF-005 already requires tests under `internal/provider/function`, focused framework unit tests, Terraform 1.8 gating, and `provider::azurerm::...` output assertions, but it does not explicitly name `resource.UnitTest` or framework provider factories.
assessments.proposedText: Provider-defined function tests belong under `internal/provider/function/*_test.go`, use `resource.UnitTest` with framework provider factories and Terraform 1.8 gating, and assert `provider::azurerm::<name>(...)` output rather than using a resource lifecycle harness.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 3 because the wrong harness or missing provider factories can make provider-defined function tests ineffective or mis-shaped; frequency is 1 because provider-defined functions are relatively rare; breadth is 1 because this applies to a narrow testing surface; hostedDetectability is 4 because file placement, `resource.UnitTest`, and provider-factory usage are all visible in diffs; evidenceStrength is 3 because the pattern is inferred from concrete upstream tests rather than a published upstream guide; falsePositiveRisk is 1 because the expected harness is precise; redundancy is 2 because the current TEST-WF-005 is close but still misses one specific safeguard, which supports an update rather than a new rule or no change.

assessments.title: Ephemeral resource `page_title` canonical format
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a deterministic frontmatter requirement for a specific documentation subtype, so Hosted can review it directly from the changed page.
assessments.summary: Add a dedicated ephemeral-resource frontmatter rule so Hosted checks the canonical `page_title` value instead of only checking that the field exists.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this rule, ephemeral-resource pages can pass current review with inconsistent titles that break reference-doc naming conventions.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: DOCS-FM-001 requires `page_title` to exist, but no active Hosted rule checks the canonical ephemeral-resource value.
assessments.proposedText: Ephemeral-resource frontmatter `page_title` must be `Azure Resource Manager: azurerm_<name>`.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 2 because the defect is mainly consistency and discoverability, not runtime correctness; frequency 2 because every new ephemeral page needs the field but the surface is still limited; breadth 1 because it affects only ephemeral-resource docs; hostedDetectability 5 because the expected string is exact; evidenceStrength 4 because the maintainer audit marked it as a genuine supplemental requirement; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the allowed value is explicit; redundancy 1 because DOCS-FM-001 checks presence but not this value, so a short new rule is justified.

assessments.title: Function `page_title` canonical format
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a precise frontmatter convention for a distinct documentation subtype, and Hosted can verify it from the markdown alone.
assessments.summary: Add a function-specific frontmatter rule so function pages use the canonical `page_title` form rather than only carrying a `page_title` field.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this rule, function reference pages can drift into resource-style titles that mislabel the documented surface.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: DOCS-FM-001 requires `page_title` to exist, but no active Hosted rule checks the function-specific value format.
assessments.proposedText: Function frontmatter `page_title` must be `Azure Resource Manager: <name>` and must not include the `azurerm_` prefix.
