assessments.proposedText: Name new service-package resource and data source files `{name}_resource.go` or `{name}_data_source.go`, and name the matching acceptance tests `{name}_resource_test.go` or `{name}_data_source_test.go`. Only keep an exception when the same service already uses an established anti-stuttering name.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity 1 fits because misnaming files is primarily a consistency issue rather than a behavioral defect; frequency 2 fits because only some changes add or rename top-level files; breadth 2 fits because the convention spans implementation and tests but mostly matters during scaffolding; hostedDetectability 5 fits because filenames and paths are explicit in diffs; evidenceStrength 4 fits because the source states exact patterns; falsePositiveRisk 4 fits because the same source acknowledges exceptions and the repository contains specialized surfaces; redundancy 3 fits because TEST-EVID-001 already covers part of the acceptance-test naming space, limiting the immediate value of a stricter standalone rule.

assessments.title: Typed resource IDs need parser, formatter, and validator support
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The glossary defines a concrete implementation contract for introducing typed Azure resource IDs, and reviewers can evaluate it when ID packages, import paths, or ID-bearing schema fields change.
assessments.summary: The glossary says a Resource ID struct should come with associated parser and formatter support, and schema fields that accept that ID type should use the corresponding validator.
assessments.impactDescription: Adding the rule would catch incomplete or inconsistent ID packages that otherwise lead to broken validation, import handling, or non-round-trippable IDs.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-SCHEMA-006 assumes a parser already exists and only governs canonical state writes; no active Hosted rule requires the full typed resource-ID contract.
assessments.proposedText: When introducing a typed Azure resource ID, define a Resource ID struct with an associated parser and formatter whose `.ID()` output round-trips through the parser. Schema fields that accept that ID type should use the associated validator unless service-specific validation requires a narrower check.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because incomplete ID definitions can break validation, import, and state handling; frequency 3 because the pattern recurs whenever new ID types or ID-accepting fields are added; breadth 4 because the contract affects schema, import, parsing, and canonicalization across services; hostedDetectability 3 because reviewers can usually see missing parser, formatter, or validator pieces in the changed ID package and schema; evidenceStrength 4 because the glossary states the association directly; falsePositiveRisk 2 because the rule can be scoped to newly introduced typed IDs and ID-bearing fields; redundancy 2 because current Hosted coverage only partially overlaps through IMPL-SCHEMA-006.

assessments.title: Case-sensitive resource ID parsing by default
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The glossary gives a specific default for parser and validator behavior that reviewers can apply whenever resource ID parsing or validation logic changes.
assessments.summary: The glossary says Azure resource IDs should parse case-sensitively by default, with case-insensitive behavior added only where a downstream requirement justifies it.
assessments.impactDescription: Adding the rule would prevent permissive parsers or validators from masking casing defects that later break Terraform or downstream Azure behavior.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-SCHEMA-006 requires canonical parsed IDs in state, but no active Hosted rule directs when parsers or validators may relax case sensitivity.
assessments.proposedText: Typed Azure resource ID parsers and validators must be case-sensitive by default. Provide a separate case-insensitive path only when a specific downstream API or import surface requires it.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because overly permissive ID parsing can hide real casing defects and destabilize state or downstream calls; frequency 3 because parser and validator logic is touched whenever new ID types are added or corrected; breadth 3 because the rule mainly affects ID helpers and schema validators rather than all implementation code; hostedDetectability 3 because reviewers can inspect parser and validator changes for case-insensitive behavior; evidenceStrength 4 because the glossary states case-sensitive parsing as the general rule and allows exceptions only when required; falsePositiveRisk 2 because the rule expressly permits evidence-backed exceptions; redundancy 2 because current Hosted rules touch ID canonicalization but not parser strictness.

assessments.title: Establish Terraform IDs in the correct lifecycle stage
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The glossary states explicit lifecycle expectations for when resources and data sources establish their Terraform IDs, and the current Hosted create/import rule already partially covers the same defect area.
assessments.summary: The glossary adds the broader expectation that resources establish IDs during create or import handling and data sources set IDs in Read, not only the current identity-specific callback case.
assessments.impactDescription: Updating the rule would catch missing or late ID establishment that breaks state tracking, import behavior, or data-source results while preserving the existing identity safeguard.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-WF-002C currently requires callback-based identity create flows to set ID and identity before returning, but it does not cover ordinary create/import ID establishment or data-source IDs.
assessments.proposedText: When Resource Identity is supported, callback-based create flows must set both the Terraform resource ID and identity before returning. More generally, a resource must establish its Terraform ID before create or import handling returns, and a data source must set its ID in Read; do not defer required ID or identity population until a later lifecycle step.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 5 because failing to establish a Terraform ID breaks state tracking and core lifecycle behavior; frequency 3 because every new resource and data source implements these paths; breadth 4 because the rule affects create, import, read, and identity flows across services; hostedDetectability 5 because missing or deferred ID establishment is usually explicit in the changed lifecycle methods; evidenceStrength 4 because the glossary states the timing directly; falsePositiveRisk 1 because the trigger is concrete and lifecycle-specific; redundancy 2 because the current rule already covers one narrow callback-based identity case, making an update better than a separate duplicate rule.

assessments.title: Add a state migration when state expectations change
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The glossary states a concrete implementation expectation for versioned state handling, and reviewers can apply it whenever a change alters what prior provider versions wrote to state.
assessments.summary: The glossary says a resource that starts expecting a different state representation should include a state migration so existing users are updated transparently.
assessments.impactDescription: Adding the rule would prevent releases from shifting state expectations without a migration, which otherwise leaves users with perpetual diffs, import churn, or manual state edits.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No active Hosted implementation rule currently requires state migrations when provider state semantics change.
assessments.proposedText: When a resource starts expecting a different state representation than prior provider versions wrote, add a state migration that rewrites existing state transparently instead of relying on manual user intervention or perpetual diffs.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 because missing state migrations can strand existing users on broken state transitions; frequency 2 because state-shape changes are less common than ordinary schema edits; breadth 3 because the issue can affect any long-lived resource type that evolves over time; hostedDetectability 3 because reviewers can compare changed state expectations against migration coverage in the diff; evidenceStrength 4 because the glossary states the need for migrations and explains the failure mode; falsePositiveRisk 2 because the rule only applies when state expectations actually change; redundancy 1 because no active Hosted rule already covers this migration requirement.

assessments.title: Prefer Terraform-managed resource IDs for new or migrated resources
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The glossary records a migration direction rather than a universally current review rule, and Hosted review would need broad architectural context to distinguish intended mixed-model work from actionable defects.
assessments.summary: The glossary says the provider is moving toward Terraform-managed resource IDs defined in `resourceids.go` instead of depending on remote API IDs.
assessments.impactDescription: If elevated to Hosted guidance, the rule would push new resources and migrations toward provider-managed IDs, but today that choice still depends on service realities and explicit migration scope.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-SCHEMA-006 covers canonical ID handling once a typed ID exists, but no active Hosted rule requires adopting Terraform-managed IDs in the first place.
assessments.proposedText: For new or migrated resources, prefer Terraform-managed resource IDs defined in `resourceids.go` over opaque API-returned IDs unless the remote service's ID is authoritative and no stable provider-managed form is viable.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 3 because ID strategy materially affects long-term state stability; frequency 2 because the decision mainly appears in new resources or explicit migrations; breadth 2 because it is narrower than general lifecycle or schema guidance; hostedDetectability 2 because a diff rarely carries enough architectural context to prove that a provider-managed ID is viable; evidenceStrength 3 because the glossary describes the direction clearly but as an ongoing migration rather than a universal present-tense mandate; falsePositiveRisk 4 because the provider intentionally mixes strategies during migration and service constraints can justify exceptions; redundancy 3 because existing Hosted ID rules already cover canonical handling once an ID design is chosen.

assessments.title: Split independent work into separate pull requests
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The source gives a concrete, reviewable PR-scoping rule with explicit examples: SDK/API upgrades, existing object field additions, and new object introductions should be separated when they are independently reviewable.
assessments.summary: Add a repository rule that keeps PRs narrowly scoped instead of bundling unrelated upgrade, extension, and new-object work together.
assessments.impactDescription: This would let Hosted flag broad PRs that combine multiple review units, reducing review noise and making implementation and test findings easier to attribute.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No active Hosted rule covers PR composition or requires independently reviewable SDK upgrades, field additions, and new objects to be split across separate PRs.
assessments.proposedText: Keep pull requests narrowly scoped. Split unrelated or independently reviewable work, such as SDK or API version upgrades, existing resource or data source field additions, and new resource or data source introductions, into separate PRs instead of bundling them together.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 3 fits because over-broad PRs degrade review quality more than they create direct runtime defects; frequency 3 fits because combined upgrade-and-feature PRs are common enough in provider work; breadth 4 fits because the guidance applies across services and object types; hostedDetectability 4 fits because mixed change classes are visible in the PR diff; evidenceStrength 5 fits because the source provides explicit normative examples; falsePositiveRisk 2 fits because genuinely coupled work can still be distinguished from avoidable bundling; redundancy 1 fits because the active catalog has no comparable repository-scoping rule.

assessments.title: Keep property reordering out of behavior-changing pull requests
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The source states a specific diff-hygiene requirement: reordering existing properties in the same PR should be avoided and moved to a follow-up change because it harms diff readability.
assessments.summary: Add a rule that separates pure property reordering from substantive implementation or documentation changes.
assessments.impactDescription: Hosted could suppress review churn from cosmetic schema and docs reflows that obscure real behavior changes in the same PR.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The active catalog has ordering rules for final documentation and schema content, but no repository rule about separating pure reordering from behavior changes in a PR.
assessments.proposedText: Do not reorder existing schema or documentation properties in a behavior-changing pull request. Pure ordering or formatting reflows must be isolated to a separate follow-up PR.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 2 fits because the primary harm is review noise rather than incorrect provider behavior; frequency 3 fits because opportunistic reorderings are a recurring cleanup pattern; breadth 3 fits because the problem spans implementation and docs but not every PR; hostedDetectability 4 fits because reorder-only hunks are easy to spot in diffs; evidenceStrength 5 fits because the source explicitly forbids this pattern; falsePositiveRisk 1 fits because substantive moves can be distinguished from pure reordering; redundancy 1 fits because no active Hosted rule addresses PR-level reorder noise.

assessments.title: Require clear, self-describing pull request titles
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The source provides direct good and bad title examples and makes title clarity an explicit maintainer expectation for review and changelog alignment.
assessments.summary: Add a PR-title rule that requires the affected area and substantive change to be obvious from the title alone.
assessments.impactDescription: This would improve triage, changelog consistency, and reviewer understanding before deeper implementation analysis starts.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No active Hosted rule governs PR title quality or rejects vague titles such as generic fixes, bare issue references, or unspecified upgrades.
assessments.proposedText: Pull request titles must clearly name the affected service, resource, data source, or subsystem and describe the substantive change. Titles that are generic, issue-only, or too vague to stand on their own are defects.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 3 fits because unclear titles materially hurt triage and review but usually not runtime correctness; frequency 4 fits because vague PR titles are a common contribution problem; breadth 5 fits because every PR has a title; hostedDetectability 5 fits because title quality is directly observable; evidenceStrength 5 fits because the source gives explicit examples and states the requirement plainly; falsePositiveRisk 2 fits because there is some judgment in what counts as specific enough but the examples anchor it well; redundancy 0 fits because the active catalog has no PR-title rule.

assessments.title: Require review-ready PR state and explanatory body context
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The source ties review readiness to non-draft status and to a PR body that explains what changed, why it changed, related issues, and testing status or blockers.
assessments.summary: Add a review-input rule for non-draft PRs with a meaningful summary, rationale, issue context when relevant, and testing evidence or blockers.
assessments.impactDescription: Hosted would have a basis to flag under-described or not-ready PRs before emitting deep implementation or testing feedback, improving evidence quality and reviewer efficiency.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: Active Hosted rules govern changed code and docs, but none require a review-ready PR body or testing context in the review input itself.
assessments.proposedText: A review-ready pull request must not be left in draft state and must provide a body that explains what changed and why, links relevant issues when applicable, and states what local checks and relevant tests were run or why they could not be run.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 4 fits because missing context and test evidence directly weakens review reliability; frequency 4 fits because incomplete PR bodies and absent testing notes are common; breadth 5 fits because this affects nearly every reviewable PR; hostedDetectability 4 fits because draft state and PR-body omissions are observable inputs; evidenceStrength 5 fits because the source includes explicit checklist items and process steps; falsePositiveRisk 2 fits because issue links are only required when applicable and the rule can preserve that condition; redundancy 1 fits because active rules cover code and docs behavior, not review-input completeness.

assessments.title: Contributor changelog entry ownership
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This source's PR template tells contributors to replace the changelog example with their entry, but the maintainer merge guide says contributors should not include changelog entries in PRs. The requirement is enforceable only after upstream ownership is resolved.
assessments.summary: Defer a contributor changelog-entry rule because current upstream guidance conflicts on whether PR bodies should contain changelog text.
assessments.impactDescription: Adding a Hosted rule now would create false positives against one of the two current upstream documents depending on which interpretation is chosen.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No active Hosted rule covers contributor changelog ownership in PR bodies, and the current upstream sources do not provide a consistent requirement to encode.
assessments.proposedText: Contributors must not place changelog entries in pull request descriptions; changelog text belongs to the maintainer merge workflow.
assessments.selectionRationale: severity 2 fits because changelog ownership affects workflow more than code correctness; frequency 2 fits because only some PRs would include changelog text; breadth 3 fits because the question touches many contribution types when it does arise; hostedDetectability 4 fits because PR-body changelog content is visible; evidenceStrength 1 fits because the two current upstream documents conflict; falsePositiveRisk 4 fits because any immediate rule would contradict one source; redundancy 1 fits because the catalog lacks a rule here, but the unresolved conflict supports defer rather than add.

assessments.title: Respect changed-field semantics in update flows
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This section gives concrete implementation guidance for resource update behavior and can be reviewed directly in changed Go resource code.
assessments.summary: The current guide requires separate create and update handling, changed-field-aware updates, and live-model merge behavior for full-update APIs; the Hosted PATCH rule only covers one stale-state omission case.
assessments.impactDescription: Expanding the rule would let Hosted reviews catch ignore_changes regressions and full-update payload defects before they ship as unexpected drift or field resets.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-PATCH-001 covers the explicit-clear requirement when omitted PATCH fields preserve remote state, but it does not currently tell reviewers to require separate update behavior or changed-field-only update payload construction.
assessments.proposedText: Use separate create and update behavior even when Azure shares one API. Update paths must respect `ignore_changes` by sending only changed patch fields, or by applying changes onto a retrieved existing model for full-update APIs. If Azure PATCH preserves omitted properties, removing Terraform configuration must still expand an explicit disabled, empty, or sentinel value instead of omitting the field and preserving stale Azure state.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 4 because broken update semantics can silently preserve stale remote values or ignore intended lifecycle behavior. Frequency is 3 because many Azure resources reuse create/update APIs. Breadth is 4 because the pattern applies across typed and legacy resources. Hosted detectability is 3 because reviewers can inspect method structure and payload construction, but API semantics still require some care. Evidence strength is 5 because the upstream guide is explicit and detailed. False positive risk is 2 because the rule still depends on distinguishing PATCH from full-update APIs, but the failure modes are concrete. Redundancy is 1 because no current Hosted rule covers the separate-handler and changed-field safeguards.

assessments.title: Use typed resources for new work and preserve the existing implementation model
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The source gives explicit implementation-model guidance that reviewers can apply when changed code introduces a new resource or modifies an existing one.
assessments.summary: The guide still says new ordinary resources and data sources should use the typed `internal/sdk` model, while changes to existing untyped resources may stay in their current model until an explicit migration.
assessments.impactDescription: Keeping the current rule unchanged preserves the model-classification safeguard that prevents reviewers from forcing the wrong abstraction on legacy, typed, or framework-native code.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-WF-001A already captures the typed-first policy for new ordinary resources and data sources, plus the safeguard to maintain the existing model unless the task is an explicit migration.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 3 because applying the wrong implementation model produces broad review mistakes and churn. Frequency is 4 because model choice comes up often in provider work. Breadth is 4 because the rule affects most implementation reviews. Hosted detectability is 5 because imports, interfaces, and file patterns make the model usually obvious. Evidence strength is 5 because the source is explicit. False positive risk is 1 because the rule is concrete and already narrowed to explicit migrations and specialized surfaces. Redundancy is 1 because the current Hosted rule already captures the needed meaning cleanly.
assessments.proposedText: Classify implementation code as legacy untyped Plugin SDK, typed `internal/sdk`, or framework-native before suggesting changes. Maintain the existing model unless the task is an explicit migration; use typed for current ordinary resource and data source work, and framework patterns for framework-native or specialized surfaces.

assessments.title: Limit Optional+Computed use and annotate unavoidable cases consistently
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is concrete schema-authoring guidance for implementation reviews, even though most of its behavioral content is already handled by broader schema rules.
assessments.summary: The guide requires contributors to avoid `Optional` plus `Computed` when `Default` or `Required` can model the behavior, and it prescribes a specific order and `// NOTE: O+C` comment format when the pattern is unavoidable.
assessments.impactDescription: Following this convention improves schema clarity and documents why an otherwise risky schema shape was chosen, but the uncovered part is mostly annotation hygiene rather than a distinct high-value Hosted defect check.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: The functional misuse of `Optional` plus `Computed` is broadly covered by IMPL-SCHEMA-001, but no Hosted rule currently enforces the exact ordering and comment-prefix convention from this guide.
assessments.proposedText: Avoid `Optional` plus `Computed` when `Default` or `Required` can model the behavior. When it is unavoidable, declare the field in `Optional`, explanatory `// NOTE: O+C ...`, `Computed` order.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 2 because the uncovered portion is mostly about documenting an already-justified schema choice. Frequency is 2 because `Optional` plus `Computed` should be relatively limited. Breadth is 3 because schema reviews do encounter the pattern across services. Hosted detectability is 4 because the schema ordering and comment prefix are easy to spot. Evidence strength is 4 because the guide is explicit. False positive risk is 1 because violations are mechanically visible. Redundancy is 4 because the important behavioral safeguard is already broadly represented by existing schema rules, leaving mainly format-level guidance.

assessments.title: Use GetRawConfig safely in CustomizeDiff when values may be unknown
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is precise diff-time validation guidance for implementation reviews and can be checked directly in changed CustomizeDiff code.
assessments.summary: The source still supports the current GetRawConfig-based rule and adds an explicit safeguard that CustomizeDiff must abstain when correctness depends on a known-after-apply value itself.
assessments.impactDescription: Adding the abstain safeguard would reduce false-positive findings and better target real CustomizeDiff defects around unknown values, especially during create-time validation.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-SCHEMA-013 already requires `GetRawConfig()`, null-vs-zero handling, and `IsKnown()` checks, but it does not currently say to abstain when the validation outcome depends on the unknown value itself.
assessments.proposedText: `CustomizeDiff` validation for optional, zero, or unknown values must inspect `GetRawConfig()`, distinguish null from configured zero values, check `IsKnown()` before traversing collections, and abstain when correctness depends on a known-after-apply value.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 4 because bad diff-time validation can block valid creates or emit incorrect errors. Frequency is 3 because unknown-value handling appears regularly in advanced schema work. Breadth is 3 because it affects a meaningful subset of implementation reviews rather than every resource. Hosted detectability is 4 because the relevant APIs and control flow are visible in diffs. Evidence strength is 5 because the guide provides a direct example and explicit conclusion. False positive risk is 1 because the new safeguard narrows the rule rather than broadening it. Redundancy is 1 because the abstain case is not already stated elsewhere in Hosted guidance.

assessments.title: Use the exact provider Go license header format
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The source defines an exact, file-level implementation convention that a reviewer could enforce directly on changed Go files.
assessments.summary: The guide mandates an exact two-line Go header at the start of the file with no preceding blank lines.
assessments.impactDescription: This convention improves repository consistency and licensing hygiene, but it is primarily a mechanically checkable formatting rule rather than a high-value semantic Hosted review guard.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No Hosted rule covers exact Go header text or blank-line placement; the current catalog intentionally focuses on higher-impact implementation defects.
assessments.proposedText: When adding or updating a Go file header, place these exact first two lines at the start of the file with no preceding blank line: `// Copyright IBM Corp. 2014, 2025` and `// SPDX-License-Identifier: MPL-2.0`.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 1 because the issue is mostly consistency rather than runtime behavior. Frequency is 2 because header edits are occasional. Breadth is 2 because it only affects Go source-file additions or header touches. Hosted detectability is 5 because the exact text and placement are trivial to inspect. Evidence strength is 5 because the source gives the exact required lines. False positive risk is 0 because compliance is mechanical. Redundancy is 5 because this sort of file-header formatting is better handled outside the limited Hosted semantic budget.

assessments.title: Prefer shared pointer helper functions over manual pointer patterns
assessments.applicabilityRationale: These are concrete implementation conventions that can be recognized in changed code, even though they mostly optimize style and consistency rather than behavior.
assessments.summary: The guide prefers `pointer.From`, `pointer.To`, and `pointer.ToEnum` over manual nil checks, temporary pointer variables, and explicit enum conversions.
assessments.impactDescription: Using the helpers improves readability and consistency, but equivalent code can still be functionally correct, so this is a weak fit for scarce Hosted semantic review capacity.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No Hosted rule covers this helper preference today, and the nearest implementation rules focus on correctness rather than local pointer idioms.
assessments.proposedText: Prefer shared pointer helpers: use `pointer.From` instead of manual nil checks, `pointer.To` instead of temporary pointer variables, and `pointer.ToEnum` instead of explicit enum conversions.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 1 because alternate code patterns are usually still correct. Frequency is 2 because pointer helpers appear regularly but not universally. Breadth is 3 because the convention can arise across many services. Hosted detectability is 4 because the helper and non-helper patterns are visible in diffs. Evidence strength is 4 because the source gives direct do-style guidance. False positive risk is 1 because the alternative patterns are easy to identify. Redundancy is 4 because the convention is stylistic and does not protect a major Hosted-specific defect class.

assessments.title: Eliminate ambiguous collection-shaped schema
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is concrete schema design guidance that can be enforced against changed implementation code when repeated collection entries can represent the same logical case.
assessments.summary: The guide explicitly says collection-typed schema should not allow multiple entries for the same semantic case when only one interpretation can make sense.
assessments.impactDescription: Adding this rule would let Hosted reviews catch ambiguous list-shaped schemas that make provider behavior depend on undefined ordering or conflicting repeated blocks.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No current Hosted rule directly flags semantically ambiguous collection shapes; IMPL-SCHEMA-001 covers validity and round-tripping broadly, but not this specific ambiguity pattern.
assessments.proposedText: Do not model a collection so Terraform can accept multiple entries for the same logical case or discriminator when only one can be meaningful. Reshape the schema to make each semantic case unambiguous.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 4 because ambiguous schema can produce confusing or unstable provider behavior without an obvious user error. Frequency is 2 because the pattern is not everywhere, but it recurs in Azure collection-shaped APIs. Breadth is 3 because multiple services expose similar modeling problems. Hosted detectability is 3 because reviewers can see duplicate semantic slots in schema design, though some domain reading is required. Evidence strength is 4 because the guide gives a clear before-and-after example. False positive risk is 2 because the defect depends on whether repeated entries are truly semantically ambiguous. Redundancy is 1 because no Hosted rule currently isolates this failure mode.

assessments.title: Model Enabled-only feature objects as booleans
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The source gives concrete schema-shape guidance for a recurring Azure pattern, so it is applicable to implementation reviews even though exceptions and judgment calls remain.
assessments.summary: The guide prefers flattening an Azure feature object to a boolean when `Enabled` is the only user-facing field, while keeping a block when `Enabled` appears with other required fields.
assessments.impactDescription: This convention improves Terraform UX consistency, but its edge cases and lower defect impact make it weaker than the current Hosted implementation priorities.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No Hosted rule currently covers `Enabled` object modeling directly; nearby schema rules focus on correctness constraints rather than this higher-level shaping preference.
assessments.proposedText: When an Azure feature object only contains an `Enabled` setting, expose it as a boolean attribute instead of a block. Keep a block when `Enabled` is configured with other required fields.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 2 because the rule mostly affects usability and consistency rather than hard correctness. Frequency is 2 because not every Azure feature uses this pattern. Breadth is 3 because it does recur across services. Hosted detectability is 3 because reviewers can see the shape, but some cases explicitly require judgment. Evidence strength is 4 because the guide explains the expected mapping with examples. False positive risk is 2 because optional companion fields make some designs less clear-cut. Redundancy is 3 because the rule overlaps with broader schema-quality review without isolating a critical Hosted-only failure mode.

assessments.title: Keep omission sentinels out of user-facing schema without erasing computed values
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is concrete schema, expand, and flatten guidance for implementation reviews and can be checked in changed schema and read/write code.
assessments.summary: The guide still requires translating user-omitted values to Azure's sentinel values, and it now makes explicit that computed-only fields must preserve the Azure-returned sentinel instead of collapsing it to omission.
assessments.impactDescription: Updating the rule would prevent Hosted reviews from over-applying the omission mapping to computed-only properties and would better align findings with the upstream guidance.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-SCHEMA-008 already covers hiding omission sentinels from user-settable schema and normalizing them through create/read paths, but it does not currently preserve the explicit computed-only exception.
assessments.proposedText: When Azure uses a `None`, `Off`, or equivalent sentinel for omission on a user-settable field, keep that sentinel out of user-facing validation, expand omitted configuration to the API sentinel, and flatten the sentinel back to omitted state. Computed-only fields should preserve the Azure-returned sentinel value.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 3 because mishandling the sentinel can create confusing state behavior, though it is usually narrower than a full lifecycle defect. Frequency is 3 because sentinel-backed omission patterns are common in Azure APIs. Breadth is 3 because several services use them. Hosted detectability is 4 because schema validators and flatten/expand logic are inspectable in diffs. Evidence strength is 5 because the guide is explicit and includes the computed-only note. False positive risk is 1 because the new exception narrows application of the rule. Redundancy is 2 because the current rule is close, but not complete.

assessments.title: Represent new SKU input as `sku` or a `sku` block
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a concrete schema-shape preference for implementation reviews, but it is mainly a consistency rule and not a strong semantic defect detector.
assessments.summary: The guide prefers new SKU inputs to use either a top-level `sku` argument or a `sku` block, instead of introducing fragmented `sku_name`-style fields for new work.
assessments.impactDescription: The convention improves consistency for users and reviewers, but most violations are UX drift rather than substantial correctness bugs, so it is a weak fit for Hosted token budget.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No Hosted rule currently covers preferred SKU field shape; existing schema rules instead focus on validation and lifecycle correctness.
assessments.proposedText: For new schema, represent SKU input as either a top-level `sku` attribute or a `sku` block when multiple SKU fields are required; do not add new fragmented `sku_name`- or `sku_family`-style inputs.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 2 because the main cost is consistency debt rather than broken behavior. Frequency is 2 because SKU design decisions are periodic, not constant. Breadth is 3 because many Azure resources expose SKU concepts. Hosted detectability is 4 because the field shape is easy to inspect. Evidence strength is 4 because the guide is clear about the preferred forms for new arguments. False positive risk is 2 because Azure SKU APIs vary and some exceptions can be reasonable. Redundancy is 3 because broader schema review already pushes toward coherent modeling without needing this extra specific rule.

assessments.title: Split discriminated resource types instead of exposing a generic `type` field
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The guidance is relevant to implementation review, but reliably applying it requires high-context architectural judgment about API inheritance, service boundaries, and acceptable exceptions.
assessments.summary: The guide prefers separate resources or data sources for discriminator-driven Azure types instead of one generic object with a wide `type` or `kind` field.
assessments.impactDescription: This can materially improve user experience and validation quality, but a Hosted rule would need sharper evidence boundaries to avoid speculative architectural findings.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No Hosted rule currently covers discriminator-driven resource splitting, and no existing rule provides the repository evidence model needed to review it safely.
assessments.proposedText: When Azure uses a discriminator such as `type` or `kind` for materially different shapes, model separate resources or data sources for each supported type instead of one generic schema that mixes all variants behind the discriminator.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 4 because exposing a generic discriminated schema can burden users and weaken validation. Frequency is 2 because true discriminator-heavy designs are not ubiquitous. Breadth is 3 because the pattern appears in multiple services. Hosted detectability is 1 because identifying the right split requires deeper API and product context than a lightweight review usually has. Evidence strength is 4 because the guide is explicit about the preference. False positive risk is 4 because many apparent discriminator cases still involve tradeoffs that are hard to judge from a diff. Redundancy is 1 because no existing Hosted rule covers this architectural decision.

assessments.title: Keep preview fields out of stable schema
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a clear implementation rule tied to schema exposure and can be reviewed directly against changed fields and API-version evidence.
assessments.summary: The source still states that preview fields should not be supported until GA, matching the current Hosted rule.
assessments.impactDescription: Keeping the rule unchanged preserves a high-value safeguard against exposing unstable Azure surface area as stable provider behavior.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-SCHEMA-007 already matches the source requirement by blocking preview-only Azure properties from stable schema unless explicit feature-gate policy allows them.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 5 because exposing preview fields as stable can create major compatibility and support risks. Frequency is 2 because true preview-field additions are intermittent. Breadth is 3 because multiple services do encounter preview APIs. Hosted detectability is 4 because API versions and field provenance are usually reviewable from code and SDK evidence. Evidence strength is 5 because the upstream statement is explicit. False positive risk is 1 because the rule already allows explicit feature-gate exceptions. Redundancy is 1 because the current Hosted rule cleanly captures the requirement.
assessments.proposedText: Do not expose preview-only Azure properties as stable schema before GA unless the provider's explicit feature-gate policy permits them.

assessments.title: Flatten single-property MaxItems-1 blocks by default
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The source offers concrete implementation guidance for schema shape, but it also depends on service-team evidence and explicit exceptions, which limits straightforward Hosted enforcement.
assessments.summary: The guide prefers flattening `MaxItems: 1` blocks that contain only one nested property unless there is evidence that more nested properties are imminent, and it asks for an inline comment when retaining the block.
assessments.impactDescription: The convention helps reduce needless nesting for users, but it is a medium-context design preference rather than a consistently high-signal semantic defect rule.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: No Hosted rule currently covers this flattening preference or its inline-comment exception model; existing schema rules focus on correctness, not this UX-oriented shaping convention.
assessments.proposedText: Flatten a `MaxItems: 1` block that contains only one nested property unless there is concrete evidence that additional nested properties are imminent. If the block stays, add an inline comment explaining why.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity is 2 because the main harm is extra nesting and inconsistency. Frequency is 2 because the pattern appears, but not in every schema review. Breadth is 2 because it affects a narrower subset of modeling decisions. Hosted detectability is 3 because the block shape is visible, but the exception depends on service-team expectations that may not be in the diff. Evidence strength is 4 because the guide states the preference clearly. False positive risk is 3 because absent evidence of imminent expansion is hard to prove. Redundancy is 2 because the rule would add a new preference area rather than reinforce a current high-value defect class.

assessments.title: Prevent empty optional blocks with all-optional nested fields
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is concrete schema validation guidance that can be reviewed directly in changed block definitions and validation wiring.

assessments.title: Prefer generated PossibleValues helpers for enum validation
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is precise implementation guidance for schema validation and can be reviewed directly in changed enum validators.
assessments.summary: The guide's validation examples still support using generated `PossibleValuesFor...()` helpers when they match the accepted enum set.
assessments.impactDescription: Keeping the current rule unchanged preserves a practical safeguard against hand-maintained enum drift while still allowing narrower validators when there is service-specific evidence.

Breadth is 3 because many services expose enum-backed fields. Hosted detectability is 4 because helper use versus manual slices is visible in diffs. Evidence strength is 5 because the source and examples clearly support the rule. False positive risk is 1 because the exception path requires explicit evidence. assessments.title: Provider error wording and wrapping
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The source is a canonical contributor guide for implementation error handling and directly prescribes the same message-shape requirements the Hosted rule enforces.
assessments.summary: The current errors guide still requires lowercase, contextual wrapping, backticks for field names and values, `%+v` for wrapped errors, and `errors.New(...)` for static strings.
assessments.impactDescription: Weakening this rule would allow user-facing provider errors to lose diagnosis context or drift from the repository's standard message format.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-ERR-001 already covers the guide's actionable requirements for casing, context, backticks, `%+v`, and `errors.New(...)` versus `fmt.Errorf(...)`.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity 4 fits broadly user-visible error defects; frequency 5 and breadth 5 reflect near-ubiquitous error handling; hostedDetectability 4 is strong from changed strings and wrappers; evidenceStrength 5 comes from the published errors guide; falsePositiveRisk 1 is low because the wording is specific; redundancy 0 supports no-change because the current Hosted rule already matches the source.
assessments.proposedText: Provider errors must be lowercase, add the operation and resource context needed to diagnose the failure, wrap field names and values in backticks, avoid contractions and terminal punctuation, and use `%+v` for underlying errors. Use `errors.New(...)` for static messages that do not wrap an error or require formatting; use `fmt.Errorf(...)` only when formatting values or wrapping context.

assessments.title: Return fully descriptive parser errors directly
assessments.applicabilityRationale: The guide explicitly says existing Resource ID parser errors can be returned unchanged because those helpers already emit standardized descriptive failures.
assessments.summary: The source still preserves the narrower rule that already-descriptive typed ID parser errors should usually be returned as-is.
assessments.impactDescription: Dropping this safeguard would encourage redundant wrapping that obscures standardized parser failures without improving diagnosis.
assessments.currentHostedCoverage: IMPL-ERR-002 already captures the guide's parser-error exception to the general wrapping rule.
assessments.selectionRationale: Severity 2 is narrower because this affects parser-call sites rather than all errors; frequency 3 and breadth 3 are moderate across Azure ID handling; hostedDetectability 4 is good because wrappers versus direct returns are visible in diffs; evidenceStrength 4 is explicit in the guide; falsePositiveRisk 1 is low because the rule is limited to already-comprehensive parser errors; redundancy 1 supports no-change because the existing Hosted rule already preserves this exception.
assessments.proposedText: Return already comprehensive typed resource ID parser errors directly. Wrap them only when the additional context materially improves diagnosis.

assessments.title: Prefix provider-internal errors with `internal-error:`
assessments.applicabilityRationale: This is a concrete implementation-facing error-message convention from the source and can be reviewed directly when code reports failed expectations or impossible internal states.
assessments.summary: The current guide still requires provider-internal errors to begin with `internal-error:` and no Hosted rule currently preserves that distinction.
assessments.impactDescription: Without this guard, provider bugs and user-actionable failures are harder to distinguish in review and in runtime diagnostics.

assessments.proposedText: If Azure PATCH preserves omitted properties, removing Terraform configuration must expand an explicit disabled, empty, or sentinel value that clears the remote feature. When both PUT and PATCH operations exist and clearing depends on sending `null`, prefer the PUT/`CreateOrUpdate` path because SDK `omitempty` serialization can omit nil PATCH fields and preserve stale Azure state.

assessments.proposedText: When the SDK exposes a `...ThenPoll` or `...CallbackThenPoll` helper for a long-running create, update, or delete, use it instead of returning after the initial request so Terraform waits for completion.

assessments.impactDescription: Keeping this rule unchanged preserves the core acceptance-test shape that proves list-resource behavior.
